docs.title: Decomposition: the flux that returns almost everything
docs.excerpt: Nearly all the carbon and nutrients that primary production takes up are returned by decomposition. Climate and litter chemistry set the pace, but a global field experiment showed that the animals doing the work matter in some climates and not others — and the standard measurement can mistake washing for decay.

docs.title: Biodiversity monitoring and ecosystem health: how scientists measure the state of life
docs.excerpt: Biodiversity has no single thermometer. This is how scientists track the condition of species and ecosystems — through field surveys, indicators, species databases, remote sensing, and long-term observation — and what each method can and cannot resolve.

docs.title: Species distribution models: what they predict, and where they stop
docs.excerpt: A model that fits a species range well in the place and period it was trained on may be worthless a valley away or a decade later. One study found temporal transferability acceptable for fewer than a quarter of species — and finer resolution made it worse, not better.

docs.title: Evapotranspiration: the largest land water flux nobody measures directly
docs.excerpt: More water leaves land as vapour than leaves it as rivers. Three independent families of global estimate now agree on the total to within about five per cent — and disagree profoundly about how much of it passes through plants.

docs.title: Land surface temperature: what the thermal band measures
docs.excerpt: A thermal satellite measures the temperature of the ground, not the air above it. In one Shanghai comparison, four accepted retrieval algorithms differed from station air temperature by between 2.39 and 12.32 degrees on the same summer day.

docs.title: Radar remote sensing: seeing through cloud, and into canopy
docs.excerpt: Optical satellites stop at the first cloud and at nightfall. Radar does neither — and because its wavelengths are centimetres rather than micrometres, it responds to structure and moisture rather than to colour.

docs.title: Soil fertility: what "available" means, and why nitrogen and phosphorus fail in opposite ways
docs.excerpt: Fertility is a rate of ion supply to a root, not a stock of nutrients sitting in the ground. That distinction explains why nitrogen is lost through mobility and phosphorus through immobility, and why recovery figures for both depend on how they were measured.

docs.title: Soil moisture: what a measurement actually covers
docs.excerpt: A satellite senses the top few centimetres of soil across a 36-kilometre cell; a probe senses a few centilitres at one point; drought decisions need the top metre. Almost every soil-moisture number in circulation is a model reconciling those three.

docs.title: Quantum sensors are leaving the lab. Here's what changes when they do.
docs.excerpt: Quantum sensors — atomic clocks, gravimeters, magnetometers — have moved from precision-physics curiosities to deployable instruments. The applications opened by the move are not the ones popular coverage emphasizes.

docs.title: Why metrology went quantum: the only standards that do not drift
docs.excerpt: Every SI unit now derives from constants realised through quantum effects, and the reason is a property no manufactured object has: identical atoms give identical results, everywhere, without calibration.

docs.title: Agroecosystems: managing an ecosystem for one output
docs.excerpt: Farmland is an ecosystem held in an early successional state by continuous inputs. Counting what goes in, what comes out and what leaks explains both its productivity and the tensions that agroecology tries to resolve.

docs.title: Biomes: how the map was drawn, and where it breaks down
docs.excerpt: A biome is a claim that macroclimate predicts vegetation form. Where the classification came from, why fire and land use put soft edges on it, and how satellite land-cover classes relate to biomes without being them.

docs.title: Ecological succession: what replaced the climax community idea
docs.excerpt: Succession is not a fixed march toward one stable endpoint. Recovery depends on what survived, what arrived and in what order — and different properties of a damaged site return on very different clocks.

docs.title: Ecosystem services: how the framework changed environmental decision-making
docs.excerpt: The phrase ecosystem services entered policy in the early 2000s. Two decades later, it has reshaped how environmental decisions get made — and where its blind spots are.

docs.title: Foundation species and the myth of functional redundancy
docs.excerpt: The claim that ecosystems are robust because species are interchangeable is comforting and largely wrong. Foundation species are how ecosystems hide their fragility.

docs.title: Primary production: what GPP, NPP and NEP measure, and how each is estimated
docs.excerpt: Gross primary production is never measured directly at ecosystem scale, only inferred. What GPP, NPP and NEP each mean, which instrument stands behind each number, and why the land and ocean halves rest on different methods.

docs.title: The soil microbiome is the missing variable in regenerative agriculture trials
docs.excerpt: Why two farms with identical practices produce different yields — and what that tells us about the next generation of soil-health metrics.

docs.title: Urban ecology: cities as ecosystems, not as the absence of one
docs.excerpt: Cities have an energy balance, a water balance and a species pool, all of them measurable. The hard part is that the two standard ways of measuring urban warming disagree by a factor of six, and city comparisons rarely control for it.

docs.title: Urban heat islands: a few degrees, unevenly distributed
docs.excerpt: US cities run about 1 to 7 °F warmer than their surroundings by day and 2 to 5 °F warmer by night, and the night figure is the one that matters. The causes are all modifications of the same surface energy balance.

docs.title: What is an ecosystem? A flow-based definition
docs.excerpt: An ecosystem is not a place — it's a flux. Here's what that distinction unlocks for thinking about resilience, restoration, and what we actually conserve.

docs.title: Remaining carbon budgets: how the number is assembled, and what it is not
docs.excerpt: A remaining carbon budget is an assessed quantity with five separately estimated components and a probability attached, not a countdown clock. The compression to a headline drops the parts that decide what it can be used for.

docs.title: Carbon-cycle feedbacks: why ocean and land sinks are not guaranteed to keep absorbing
docs.excerpt: Land and ocean absorb roughly half of human carbon emissions today. Whether they keep doing so is among the largest uncertainties in long-term climate projection.

docs.title: Adaptation and mitigation indicators: tracking action alongside climate state
docs.excerpt: Indicators of adaptation progress and mitigation effort are reported separately from physical-climate indicators, and they have different methodological constraints. Here is what each one measures.

docs.title: Climate indicators and Earth system monitoring: how the signals fit together
docs.excerpt: Climate indicators track the state of the Earth system. Here is how temperature, ocean heat, greenhouse gases, sea level, and ice are read together, and what each is good for.

docs.title: Climate models and projections: where the uncertainty actually comes from
docs.excerpt: A projection range is not a forecast with error bars. It combines scenario, model-structural, and internal-variability uncertainty, and the shares shift over time.

docs.title: Climate sensitivity: what ECS and TCR measure, and how AR6 narrowed the range
docs.excerpt: Equilibrium climate sensitivity and the transient climate response answer different questions about the same system. This is what each holds fixed, how four lines of evidence were combined, and why the thermometer record alone reads low.

docs.title: Cryosphere indicators: glaciers, sea ice, ice sheets, and snow cover
docs.excerpt: Sea-ice extent, glacier mass balance, ice-sheet loss, snow cover, permafrost. Each measures a different frozen reservoir and responds on a different timescale.

docs.title: Extreme-weather attribution: how scientists link specific events to climate change
docs.excerpt: Attribution science quantifies how much a specific extreme event was made more likely or more severe by climate change. The methods are well-defined, and so are the limits of what they can say.

docs.title: Global temperature records: what GISTEMP, HadCRUT, NOAAGlobalTemp, and reanalyses each measure
docs.excerpt: There is no single global temperature dataset. There are several, built independently from overlapping observations. Here is what each one does and why they mostly agree.

docs.title: Greenhouse-gas concentrations: how the global monitoring works
docs.excerpt: Atmospheric CO₂, methane, and nitrous oxide are tracked by a global flask network anchored at Mauna Loa, plus satellite columns and the WMO global mean. Here is how the records are built.

docs.title: Greenhouse gases and radiative forcing: what the term actually measures
docs.excerpt: Radiative forcing is the bookkeeping unit that lets atmospheric scientists compare the climate effect of one molecule against another. It is also the unit most commonly misread.

docs.title: Heat limits and the wet-bulb threshold: why 35 °C was never measured
docs.excerpt: The famous survivability limit came from a thermodynamic argument, not from people. When the experiment was finally done, the threshold in warm humid conditions came out near 30.6 °C, and the reasons it is lower are all physiological.

docs.title: Heat mortality and what the records count: why the official figure is a floor
docs.excerpt: The United States recorded an average of 702 heat deaths a year from 2004 to 2018. That number comes from death certificates, and death certificates record the immediate cause rather than the weather that precipitated it.

docs.title: Ocean heat content: the climate indicator the atmosphere can't hide
docs.excerpt: Surface air temperature is noisy. The ocean is not. What ocean heat content measures, and why it is treated as the most stable indicator of climate-system warming.

docs.title: Sea-level rise: which indicator answers which question
docs.excerpt: Global mean sea level, local sea level, and the rate of rise are three different indicators. Each answers a different question, and they are reported by different agencies for different reasons.

docs.title: How temperate forests are quietly losing their carbon sink capacity
docs.excerpt: Long-term inventory networks show why temperate forest carbon sinks should be treated as dynamic and disturbance-sensitive, not as guaranteed offsets.

docs.title: What is climate change? The mechanism, the evidence, and the open questions
docs.excerpt: Climate change refers to the long-term shift in Earth's energy balance driven by changes in atmospheric composition. Here's the mechanism, the evidence behind it, and the questions that remain genuinely open.

docs.title: Biodiversity baselines and shifting baselines: choosing the reference for change
docs.excerpt: Every statement about biodiversity loss is measured against a baseline, and the choice of baseline quietly determines the verdict. This explains shifting-baseline syndrome, why it makes degraded systems look normal, and how scientists try to reconstruct deeper reference conditions.

docs.title: Biodiversity indicators explained: how a multi-dimensional thing is reported
docs.excerpt: Because no single number captures biodiversity, monitoring distils the data into indicators. This maps the main ones — extinction risk, population abundance, habitat extent, and ecosystem intactness — and explains why they are read together rather than collapsed into one figure.

docs.title: Citizen-science biodiversity data: scale, bias, and how it is corrected
docs.excerpt: Volunteer observers now generate a large share of the world’s species records. This explains how that data reaches scientific use through aggregators like GBIF, where its spatial and taxonomic biases come from, and the statistical methods used to make uneven, opportunistic observations usable.

docs.title: Ecological integrity indicators: measuring whether an ecosystem is still intact
docs.excerpt: Ecological integrity asks whether an ecosystem still has the species, structure, and processes characteristic of its type. This covers the composite indicators used to estimate it — Biodiversity Intactness, mean species abundance, indices of biotic integrity — and why the reference state is the hard part.

docs.title: Ecosystem resilience indicators: measuring the capacity to absorb disturbance
docs.excerpt: Resilience is an ecosystem capacity, not a state, which makes it hard to measure directly. This explains how scientists approximate it — through functional and response diversity, recovery rates, and statistical early-warning signals of approaching regime shifts — and why those signals are not guarantees.

docs.title: Essential Biodiversity Variables: making monitoring comparable across the globe
docs.excerpt: Biodiversity is harder to monitor than climate because no single instrument captures it. Essential Biodiversity Variables are the framework that makes the patchwork comparable.

docs.title: Habitat fragmentation metrics: measuring how landscapes break apart
docs.excerpt: Habitat loss and habitat fragmentation are related but distinct, and conflating them produces bad conclusions. This explains the landscape metrics — patch size, edge, core area, and connectivity — used to quantify fragmentation, and the live scientific debate about how much it matters independently of habitat amount.

docs.title: The Living Planet Index explained: what an average population trend measures
docs.excerpt: The Living Planet Index aggregates thousands of vertebrate population time series into a single trend. Understanding what it is — a relative average, not a headcount of animals — and the methodological debates around it is essential to reading the headline figure correctly.

docs.title: Protected-area effectiveness: why coverage is not the same as outcome
docs.excerpt: The share of land and sea inside protected areas is rising, but designation does not guarantee results. This explains how effectiveness is actually assessed — management evaluations and counterfactual impact studies — and why a protected area on a map can still be a "paper park".

docs.title: Remote sensing for biodiversity monitoring: what satellites can and cannot see
docs.excerpt: Satellites cannot see most species, but they measure the structure of ecosystems consistently and globally. This explains what Earth observation actually contributes to biodiversity monitoring — land cover, canopy structure, vegetation state — and the limits of inferring biological diversity from a spectral signal.

docs.title: Species evenness and diversity indices: why a count is not enough
docs.excerpt: Two communities with the same number of species can differ sharply in how abundance is shared among them. Evenness, and the Shannon, Simpson, and Hill-number diversity indices that combine it with richness, capture what a raw count leaves out.

docs.title: Species richness explained: what a count of species can and cannot tell you
docs.excerpt: Species richness is the simplest biodiversity measure and the easiest to misread. Here is what a count of species actually represents, how sampling effort and area distort it, and the estimators used to make counts comparable.

docs.title: Why species counts mislead conservation prioritization
docs.excerpt: Species richness is the easiest biodiversity metric to compute and the worst one to prioritize on. Functional and phylogenetic diversity are what predict ecosystem performance — and they often disagree with the species count.

docs.title: Biogeochemical cycles: reservoirs, fluxes, and the arithmetic that makes them comparable
docs.excerpt: Carbon, water, and nitrogen move through the planet on wildly different schedules. One ratio — reservoir divided by flux — explains most of the difference.

docs.title: Biosphere–climate interactions: when vegetation cools the ground and warms the planet
docs.excerpt: Plants affect climate through carbon, water, and reflectivity at once, and the three effects do not always point the same way. That is why afforestation arithmetic is regional.

docs.title: The carbon cycle: where the carbon is, how it moves, and what changed
docs.excerpt: Most of Earth's carbon is locked in rock and moves on geological time. A small fast-cycling fraction runs through air, water, and life — and that is the part we changed.

docs.title: Climate feedbacks: the arithmetic that turns a small push into a large response
docs.excerpt: A feedback is not a vague amplification. It is a number in watts per square metre per degree, it has a sign convention, and IPCC AR6 publishes the assessed value for each one.

docs.title: Modes of variability and teleconnections: internal oscillations versus forced change
docs.excerpt: Some of what moves in the climate record is being pushed; some is the system oscillating on its own. Telling them apart is a defined statistical problem.

docs.title: The cryosphere as an active component: four ways ice changes the rest of the system
docs.excerpt: Ice is usually presented as something the climate does things to. It is also a component that changes reflectivity, sea level, ocean density, and the carbon cycle in return.

docs.title: The five components of the Earth system, and why their boundaries leak
docs.excerpt: Atmosphere, hydrosphere, cryosphere, biosphere, geosphere. The split is a working convention, and knowing where it breaks down is more instructive than memorising it.

docs.title: Earth system models: what gets added when a climate model becomes an ESM
docs.excerpt: An Earth system model is a coupled climate model with the biogeochemistry made interactive. That one change alters what it can be asked, and where it goes wrong.

docs.title: Predictability across timescales: why two weeks is hard and a century is not
docs.excerpt: A forecast and a projection are different kinds of statement. One depends on knowing today's state precisely; the other does not, which is why the longer one can be more reliable.

docs.title: Earth system science: how the planet's major systems interact
docs.excerpt: Air, water, ice, rock, and life are usually studied apart. Earth system science studies the couplings between them — where most of the behaviour and most of the uncertainty live.

docs.title: Earth-system tipping points: what IPCC AR6 actually assesses, element by element
docs.excerpt: The popular version treats tipping points as one looming threshold. IPCC AR6 treats them as fifteen separate questions, with confidence ranging from high to low.

docs.title: ENSO explained: how a wind–ocean loop in the Pacific reaches the rest of the world
docs.excerpt: El Niño and La Niña are the two phases of one coupled oscillation. NOAA defines them with a specific index, a specific box of ocean, and a specific persistence rule.

docs.title: Essential Climate Variables: the 55-item list that decides what gets measured
docs.excerpt: GCOS specifies 55 variables the world has agreed to observe continuously. The selection criteria are as informative as the list — and one of them is not scientific importance.

docs.title: The global water cycle: a tiny reservoir with an enormous throughput
docs.excerpt: The atmosphere holds a thousandth of one per cent of Earth's water and replaces it about forty times a year. That mismatch shapes how the water cycle responds to warming.

docs.title: The ice-albedo feedback: small in the global mean, dominant at the poles
docs.excerpt: Losing bright ice and exposing dark ocean amplifies warming. The mechanism is simple, the global number is smaller than assumed, and the regional effect is where it counts.

docs.title: Model intercomparison as a measurement device: what a multi-model spread is for
docs.excerpt: CMIP exists because no single climate model can be validated against a second Earth. Running many models under identical forcing turns disagreement between them into a measurable quantity, which is a substitute for a control and not the same thing as one.

docs.title: The nitrogen cycle: an inert ocean of gas and the thin reactive stream that matters
docs.excerpt: Nitrogen is the most abundant gas in the air and among the scarcest nutrients in most ecosystems. The paradox lives in the chemistry of breaking a single bond.

docs.title: Nutrient stoichiometry and the Redfield ratio: a constant that is not constant
docs.excerpt: Marine organic matter has an average carbon-to-nitrogen-to-phosphorus ratio near 106:16:1, and models have used it as a constant for eighty years. A global compilation puts the median N:P at 22, and the deviations are systematic by region.

docs.title: The phosphorus cycle: the element with no atmosphere to fall back on
docs.excerpt: Carbon, nitrogen and sulphur all have gas phases that let them move globally and be replenished from the air. Phosphorus does not, and every consequence of that follows from one missing reservoir.

docs.title: The water-vapour feedback, and why it is always quoted with the lapse rate
docs.excerpt: Water vapour is the strongest amplifier in the climate system and not a driver of it. The two facts are compatible, and the reason is a nine-day residence time.

docs.title: Drought monitoring systems: measuring water deficit from the ground and space
docs.excerpt: Drought is monitored with a combination of climate indices and satellite measurements of rain, soil moisture, vegetation, and groundwater. This explains the main drought indices, the satellite inputs, the operational observatories, and why no single number defines a drought.

docs.title: Earth observation and remote sensing explained: how the planet is measured from space
docs.excerpt: Satellites have become the instruments that let scientists watch the whole planet at once. This explains how Earth observation works — from photons to calibrated data products — what it measures across climate and ecosystems, and where its limits lie.

docs.title: Fluorescence as a measure of photosynthesis: reading the light plants give back
docs.excerpt: Vegetation re-emits a faint glow that greenness indices cannot see, and it tracks the light reactions rather than the leaf area. Two satellites now measure it globally, and they agree with each other.

docs.title: Land-cover change detection: mapping how the surface changes over time
docs.excerpt: Comparing satellite images from different dates is how large-scale land change is measured. This explains the difference between land cover and land use, the main change-detection methods, the global products, and the errors that have to be controlled.

docs.title: MODIS: the daily global view of the Earth system
docs.excerpt: For over two decades the MODIS instruments on NASA’s Terra and Aqua satellites have imaged the entire planet almost every day. This explains the sensor, its 36 bands and coarse-but-frequent coverage, the products it generates, and its VIIRS successors.

docs.title: Ocean-colour observations: reading the sea from its colour
docs.excerpt: The colour of the ocean carries information about the microscopic plants living in it. This explains how satellites estimate phytoplankton from water-leaving light, the missions that have built the record, and why atmospheric correction over water is the hard part.

docs.title: Satellite deforestation monitoring: detecting forest loss from orbit
docs.excerpt: Satellites are the primary way forest loss is detected at scale, from annual global statistics to near-real-time clearing alerts. This explains how the change is measured from image time series, who reports it, and the uncertainties that come with monitoring tropical forests from space.

docs.title: Sensor calibration and record continuity: how a fifty-year satellite archive stays comparable
docs.excerpt: A climate record assembled from successive satellites is only a record if the instruments agree. Keeping them agreeing means reprocessing the whole archive when the calibration improves — which is why the data you downloaded last year may not be the data available now.

docs.title: The Sentinel satellites explained: the eyes of Copernicus
docs.excerpt: The Sentinel fleet is the satellite backbone of Europe’s Copernicus programme. This explains what each Sentinel family measures — radar, multispectral optical, ocean and land colour, atmospheric composition, and sea level — and why free, frequent data changed operational monitoring.

docs.title: What is remote sensing? Measuring the planet without touching it
docs.excerpt: Remote sensing means measuring a surface from a distance by recording the radiation it reflects or emits. This explains the physics — passive and active sensors, the spectral bands, and the four kinds of resolution — that make satellite measurement of the environment possible.

docs.title: Community and Indigenous-managed lands: what outcome studies can and cannot attribute
docs.excerpt: Land under community or Indigenous management is never randomly located, so simple comparisons overstate what management achieved. Matched designs shrink the estimates without erasing them.

docs.title: Conservation science: what the evidence base actually supports
docs.excerpt: Conservation is an applied science built on a causal question: did the action change the trajectory? This page sets out how that question is tested, what the syntheses currently support, and where the evidence runs out.

docs.title: Prioritisation: what changes when conservation is treated as a budget problem
docs.excerpt: Ranking species by how threatened they are does not tell anyone where to spend. Complementarity, cost and probability of success reorder the list, and an area target can be met without ecological gain.

docs.title: Ecological restoration: what the meta-analyses show, and what counts as success
docs.excerpt: Restoration reliably improves on a degraded baseline and reliably falls short of a reference one. Which comparison a study makes decides the verdict, and few projects are watched long enough to settle it.

docs.title: Reintroduction and captive breeding: reading the record on species recovery
docs.excerpt: Releasing animals is not the same as recovering a population. The translocation record, the genetics of small populations and the best-documented rescues all point at the same gap between the two.

docs.title: Invasive species: which management interventions have evidence behind them
docs.excerpt: Most introduced organisms never become invasive, and the cleanest effectiveness evidence comes from island eradications. This page separates what the intervention record supports from what the global cost figures can carry.

docs.title: Mineral demand and conservation trade-offs: where the transition meets the map
docs.excerpt: Decarbonisation needs materials, materials need mines, and mines occupy specific places. The conservation question is not whether to accept impact but how siting decisions are made — and the tools for making them well already exist.

docs.title: Rewilding: one word, three research programmes, and an uneven evidence base
docs.excerpt: Trophic, passive and Pleistocene rewilding share a name but not a method, a reference state or a literature. Separating them is what makes the evidence, and the gaps in it, legible.

docs.title: How extinction risk is assessed, and what a Red List category means
docs.excerpt: A Red List category states a probability of extinction under defined criteria, not ecological importance or rarity. This is what the five criteria require, why Data Deficient is not a threat category, and how uneven the coverage is.

docs.title: Air-sea gas exchange: the number that sets how fast the ocean takes up carbon
docs.excerpt: Ocean carbon uptake is computed from a concentration difference multiplied by a transfer velocity, and the transfer velocity is the weak link. Wind speed alone explains about a third of its short-term variability.

docs.title: Coral reefs: the symbiosis, the heat-stress metric, and the recovery record
docs.excerpt: Bleaching is the collapse of a nutritional partnership, not the death of a colony. This explains the symbiosis that fails, how degree heating weeks quantify the stress that breaks it, and what the recovery and restoration evidence supports.

docs.title: The deep sea: the largest habitat on Earth, and the least sampled
docs.excerpt: More than nine-tenths of the ocean lies below the sunlit layer, and explorers have directly seen less than a thousandth of a per cent of its floor. This is what depth does to life, and how much of the reasoning about it rests on inference.

docs.title: How a fish stock assessment is built, and why two assessments of the same ocean disagree
docs.excerpt: A stock assessment is a fitted model, not a census. This page follows the three data streams it runs on, the reference points it produces, the stocks nobody assesses at all, and why two analyses of the same database reached opposite conclusions.

docs.title: Light in the ocean: why photosynthesis stops at 200 metres
docs.excerpt: Light is detectable a kilometre down and useful for photosynthesis in only the top fifth of that. The three zones the ocean is divided into are defined by that fact, and almost everything about deep-sea biology follows from it.

docs.title: Marine productivity: how a gigatonne of algae feeds five gigatonnes of animals
docs.excerpt: The ocean supports more consumer biomass than producer biomass, which sounds impossible until you account for turnover. This works through the arithmetic, the nutrient limits, and what satellite ocean colour can and cannot see.

docs.title: Marine protected areas: the evidence tracks protection level, not area
docs.excerpt: Fully protected reserves, partially protected zones and unenforced designations all count as marine protected area on a map, and their measured effects differ by more than an order of magnitude. Averaging across them is how the evidence gets misread.

docs.title: Ocean acidification: the carbonate chemistry, and what the biology actually shows
docs.excerpt: Dissolving CO₂ in seawater adds carbon while removing carbonate ions, which is the whole problem in one sentence. Here is the measured chemistry, the saturation states that follow from it, and where laboratory and field biology part company.

docs.title: Deoxygenation: coastal dead zones and open-ocean oxygen loss are not the same problem
docs.excerpt: Two processes are routinely reported under one heading. Coastal hypoxia is driven by nutrient loading and stratification and can reverse within years; open-ocean oxygen decline is driven by warming and circulation and works on a different timescale.

docs.title: Ocean science: how depth organises the sea, and how little of it we watch
docs.excerpt: Density sorts seawater into layers that exchange slowly, and nearly every large-scale property of the sea follows from that sorting. This is what the layering does to chemistry and life, and how thinly the ocean is actually observed.

docs.title: Stratification, mixing and nutrient supply: why sunlit water can be barren
docs.excerpt: Photosynthesis happens where the light is and nutrients accumulate where it is dark. Whether the two meet depends on how strongly the water column is layered, which is why the most productive parts of the ocean are the windy ones.

docs.title: Dams and river fragmentation: barriers, sediment starvation and the removal record
docs.excerpt: Nobody knows how many barriers fragment the world's rivers, and the ones that dominate the count are too small to appear in any register. What follows from that, for connectivity, sediment, greenhouse gases and the evidence from dam removal.

docs.title: Freshwater biodiversity decline: what the abundance indices measure and how far they carry
docs.excerpt: The freshwater Living Planet Index reports the steepest decline of any realm, and it is also the index whose value depends most visibly on analytical choices. This page separates what the data show from what the summary statistic asserts.

docs.title: Freshwater ecosystems: under 0.01% of the water, over 10% of described species
docs.excerpt: Rivers, lakes and swamps hold under a hundredth of a per cent of the water on Earth and wet a few per cent of the land, yet they carry more than a tenth of all described species. That mismatch shapes everything about them.

docs.title: Groundwater: how depletion is measured, and why the methods disagree
docs.excerpt: Groundwater holds most of the planet's liquid fresh water, yet its condition can only be inferred. Wells, satellite gravimetry and hydrological models each measure something different, and the gaps between them explain most published disagreements.

docs.title: Lakes: stratification, phosphorus, and why recovery lags the cleanup
docs.excerpt: Density stratification, not chemistry, is the first fact about a deep lake. Whole-lake experiments identified phosphorus as the lever on eutrophication, but sediment stores and bistable shallow systems mean cutting the load rarely buys a quick recovery.

docs.title: Wetlands: what they do, and why the loss figure keeps changing
docs.excerpt: A wetland is identified by hydrology, soil and vegetation, and where those thresholds sit decides the statistic. The most systematic global reconstruction puts inland wetland loss since 1700 at 21 per cent, well below earlier extrapolations, and the gap is methodological.

docs.title: Boreal forests: the carbon is in the ground, and the inventories stop above it
docs.excerpt: Northern forest carbon sits mostly in cold, wet, slowly decomposing soil and in the permafrost beneath it — a pool that standard forest inventory conventions measure to a shallow, country-chosen depth or not at all.

docs.title: Deforestation statistics: why credible sources report different numbers
docs.excerpt: Country reporting and satellite tree-cover products measure different quantities under the same headline word. This explains what each one counts, why neither is the more accurate of the two, and how to read a deforestation figure without over-reading it.

docs.title: Measuring forest carbon: allometry, plots, lidar, and the error budget
docs.excerpt: Nobody weighs a forest. Every published forest-carbon figure is the output of a chain of substitutions running from a tape measure to a global total, and the largest pool in that total is the one measured worst.

docs.title: Degradation is not deforestation, and it is much harder to see
docs.excerpt: A stand can lose most of its carbon and much of its biodiversity while staying inside the forest category in every official statistic. Here is why the process resists definition, why optical satellites miss it, and what the carbon evidence supports.

docs.title: Forest disturbance regimes: fire, insects, wind, and records that will not add up
docs.excerpt: Disturbance is how forests work, not an interruption of it. The global reporting on it is patchy enough that the compilers decline to give a world total, which changes how every published disturbance figure should be read.

docs.title: Forests: structure, function, and the definitions that decide the statistics
docs.excerpt: A forest is a land-use category before it is an ecosystem, and the thresholds in that category decide most of the numbers published about it. This page sets out the definitions, the structure they describe, and where the global picture runs out.

docs.title: Planting trees: what regrowth, plantations and the global restoration estimates can support
docs.excerpt: A single 2019 estimate of global tree-restoration potential drew five formal technical comments and an erratum. Working through what was disputed is the fastest route into what the restoration evidence does and does not carry.

docs.title: Tropical forest diversity: the coexistence problem and what long-term plots have tested
docs.excerpt: Why competitive exclusion has not thinned lowland tropical tree communities is an open question with three serious candidate answers. This page sets out what the permanent-plot networks have actually been able to test, and what they have not.

docs.title: Land degradation: a contested concept with real consequences
docs.excerpt: Global assessments put somewhere between a fifth and two-fifths of land in a degraded condition. The range comes from three choices — what degradation means, what it is measured against, and which indicator is trusted.

docs.title: Nutrient losses and use efficiency: what happens to fertiliser that the crop does not take
docs.excerpt: A large share of applied nitrogen and phosphorus leaves the field, and the two leave by different routes for reasons rooted in their chemistry. That difference decides which interventions work for which element.

docs.title: The soil food web: the most species-rich habitat and the least catalogued
docs.excerpt: Nematodes alone number about 4.4 × 10²⁰ individuals worldwide. The organisms below ground build most of the carbon that persists there, and the molecular methods used to survey them are systematically misleading in known ways.

docs.title: Soil carbon: why the measurement problem is the whole problem
docs.excerpt: Global estimates of carbon in the top 30 centimetres of soil range from 504 to 1,267 petagrams. The spread is not disagreement about the soil but about depth, bulk density, sampling density and what counts as a measurement.

docs.title: Soil erosion: three processes, and why measured and modelled rates disagree
docs.excerpt: Water, wind and tillage strip land by different mechanisms and are quantified by different methods. The resulting global rates span two orders of magnitude, and most of that spread belongs to the methods rather than to the fields.

docs.title: How a soil profile forms, and why two classification systems both survive
docs.excerpt: Weathering, translocation and organic accumulation leave layers that pedologists read as a record of process. Naming those layers is a second problem, and the two dominant systems persist because they were built to answer different questions.

docs.title: Soil: the slowest-forming resource most terrestrial life depends on
docs.excerpt: Soil is a four-phase system organised into horizons, built at a median rate near 0.15 tonnes per hectare a year. That rate, and the difficulty of measuring what soil holds, shapes every argument about it.

docs.title: Air quality: what the monitors measure and what the index hides
docs.excerpt: A regulatory air measurement is a concentration plus a statistical form, and the index built on top of it keeps only the worst pollutant. Both steps discard information that matters for reading any air quality claim.

docs.title: Detection limits and non-detects: what a result of "not detected" actually means
docs.excerpt: A non-detect is not a zero, and how a dataset treats it changes the average. EPA's guidance names four ways of handling the problem and says which of them is biased in which direction.

docs.title: Pollution: source, pathway, receptor — the framework that organises the evidence
docs.excerpt: A substance becomes pollution only when a source, a pathway and a receptor line up. That triad, and the dose–response step at its centre, explains why environmental limits differ between countries without the underlying science differing.

docs.title: Microplastics: strong evidence of presence, thin evidence of harm
docs.excerpt: Microplastic particles are found almost everywhere anyone looks for them. Whether they cause ecological or human harm at the concentrations actually measured in the environment is a far weaker claim, and largely for methodological reasons.

docs.title: Reactive nitrogen: one element, a cascade of separate problems
docs.excerpt: Human activity now fixes about as much reactive nitrogen as the whole natural biosphere, and a single atom can drive air pollution, acidification, coastal hypoxia and greenhouse forcing in sequence — on clocks that run from weeks to centuries.

docs.title: Noise and artificial light at night: pollution that cannot be sampled after the fact
docs.excerpt: Sound and light leave no residue in soil, water or tissue. They exist only while the source is running, and that single property shapes how they are measured, why their ecological effects were regulated late, and what the evidence can support.

docs.title: Particulate matter: the strongest environmental-health evidence base, and its limits
docs.excerpt: Fine particles are defined by size rather than composition, and the cohort evidence linking them to mortality is the most replicated in environmental epidemiology. What remains unresolved is the shape of the curve at low concentrations.

docs.title: ATP and cellular energy budgets: what the numbers per second actually are
docs.excerpt: A human cell turns over ten million to a hundred million ATP molecules a second, and most of that goes on making protein rather than on anything that looks like activity. The budget is more informative than the pathway diagram.

docs.title: Cell division: one process copies, the other deliberately shuffles
docs.excerpt: Mitosis and meiosis are usually taught as variants of one mechanism. They solve opposite problems — faithful duplication against engineered variation — and the checkpoints, the error rates and the disease consequences all follow from that difference.

docs.title: The cell membrane: self-assembly, selectivity, and the price of a gradient
docs.excerpt: A lipid bilayer builds itself and then leaks almost nothing. What a cell spends to keep its interior chemically unlike its surroundings, and how channels, carriers and pumps divide that work, is the substance of membrane biology.

docs.title: Cell signaling: how cells decide what to do next
docs.excerpt: A cell receives thousands of signals every second. The mechanisms by which it weighs them and acts coherently are among the most studied — and still partially open — questions in cell biology.

docs.title: Coral microbiomes and the second mechanism of bleaching resistance
docs.excerpt: Beyond Symbiodinium shuffling, the bacterial community surrounding coral tissue appears to mediate heat tolerance — and it can be partially seeded.

docs.title: The cytoskeleton: three polymers, and why only two of them burn fuel
docs.excerpt: Actin filaments, microtubules and intermediate filaments differ in diameter, subunit and job, but the deep division is nucleotide hydrolysis. Two of the three spend energy to stay unstable, and that instability is what makes them useful.

docs.title: Light harvesting and photosystem efficiency: the most efficient converter in nature
docs.excerpt: Photosystem I converts nearly every absorbed photon into a charge separation. That near-perfect internal efficiency sits inside an overall process that is famously inefficient, and the gap between the two is where the interesting biology is.

docs.title: Cellular respiration: follow the electrons, not the sugar
docs.excerpt: Respiration is usually taught as a sequence of pathways to memorise. Read instead as a controlled fall of electrons down 1.14 volts, with a proton gradient as the intermediate currency, and the textbook ATP totals stop looking like constants.

docs.title: Photosynthesis: a photochemical device bolted to a slow enzyme
docs.excerpt: The light reactions are among the fastest and most efficient energy conversions in biology. The carbon-fixing enzyme they feed is one of the slowest and least specific. Most of what plants do about photosynthesis is a response to that mismatch.

docs.title: Ultraviolet damage and repair: why 5 per cent of the UV does most of the harm
docs.excerpt: UVA is 95 per cent of the ultraviolet reaching the ground and UVB is 5 per cent, and it is the 5 per cent that DNA absorbs. Humans repair the resulting lesions by cutting them out, because the enzyme that would simply undo them was lost.

docs.title: What is a cell? The unit of life, defined operationally
docs.excerpt: A cell is the smallest unit that can sustain itself, copy itself, and respond to its environment. Each of those requirements rules out what "cell" doesn't mean — and explains why borderline cases are interesting.

docs.title: DNA damage and repair after radiation: two pathways and a decision about which to use
docs.excerpt: A double-strand break can be rejoined quickly and imperfectly, or slowly and accurately using a sister chromatid as a template. Which happens depends on where in the cell cycle the break occurs, and the choice is actively made.

docs.title: Replication and repair: fidelity assembled from three imperfect filters
docs.excerpt: Copying a genome with roughly one error per ten billion bases is not a property of the chemistry. It is what polymerase selectivity, proofreading and mismatch repair produce when they act in series, backed by repair that never stops.

docs.title: Epigenetics: what the term means, and the claims it cannot support
docs.excerpt: Epigenetics carries a strict laboratory definition and a much looser popular one. This page separates them, works through the cases where the strict definition clearly holds, and explains why transgenerational claims in mammals remain weakly supported.

docs.title: Genome-wide association studies: what an association can and cannot establish
docs.excerpt: A GWAS correlates allele frequency with a trait across unrelated people. The design is deliberately hypothesis-free, and almost every limit it has — tagging, thresholds, tiny effects, poor portability — follows directly from that choice.

docs.title: Heritability: what a figure like 0.8 actually describes
docs.excerpt: Heritability is a ratio of variances estimated in one population under one range of environments. It is not a measure of how genetically fixed a trait is, and it carries no information about differences between groups.

docs.title: Gene expression regulation: why two cells with the same genome are not the same cell
docs.excerpt: A liver cell and a neuron carry identical DNA. The reason they are not interchangeable is regulation — a layered system of decisions about which genes are read and when.

docs.title: Mutation: how much, of what kind, and how much of it matters
docs.excerpt: Mutation covers events spanning eight orders of magnitude in size. Trio sequencing has pinned the human germline rate near 1.2 × 10⁻⁸ per base per generation, and the same datasets show why most of what it produces is harmless.

docs.title: Single-cell sequencing is rewriting evolutionary developmental biology
docs.excerpt: Cell-type atlases across species are revealing that the conserved unit of evolution may be the cell type, not the gene network.

docs.title: What a genome is, and why its size tells you almost nothing
docs.excerpt: A genome is the complete DNA content of a cell. Size, gene count and functional fraction are three separate measurements answering three separate questions, and they have very different reliability.

docs.title: What is DNA? The molecule, the code, and what it doesn't determine
docs.excerpt: DNA is a four-letter molecular code that stores the information needed to build and run a cell. Understanding what it does — and the equally important things it does not do — is the foundation of modern biology.

docs.title: Antibiotic resistance: how evolution outpaces drug development
docs.excerpt: Antimicrobial resistance is one of the clearest contemporary examples of evolution acting on a human timescale. The mechanisms — and what they say about how evolution actually works — are well-characterized.

docs.title: Cell types as the conserved unit of animal evolution
docs.excerpt: If cell types — not organs or networks — are what selection conserves, the standard textbook story about animal evolution needs structural revision.

docs.title: Convergent evolution: what repeated solutions do and do not tell us
docs.excerpt: Unrelated lineages arrive at similar traits often enough that convergence is used as evidence of adaptation and as a guide to causal mutations. It is also generated in quantity by chance, which makes the null model the hard part.

docs.title: Evolution: the mechanisms, the evidence, and the questions still open
docs.excerpt: Evolution is change in the genetic composition of populations, and four processes drive it rather than one. This page sets out the mechanisms, the independent evidence behind common descent, and what the live arguments are actually about.

docs.title: Genetic drift: why population size decides whether selection matters
docs.excerpt: Drift is the allele-frequency change that comes from finite sampling alone. Because its strength scales inversely with effective population size, that one parameter decides which selection coefficients are visible to evolution and which are invisible.

docs.title: Horizontal gene transfer and the tree: a forest with a current running through it
docs.excerpt: Gene gain and loss in microbes runs at a rate comparable to point mutation and at least ten times the duplication rate. That should destroy the tree of life, and the striking finding is that a consensus topology still explains nearly 40 per cent of the variance.

docs.title: Sexual selection: the mechanisms, the measurements, and the open disputes
docs.excerpt: Competition for mates explains traits that survival cannot. The comparative evidence for stronger sexual selection in males is reasonably firm; the reasons females prefer particular males, and the standards used to decide, are not.

docs.title: Speciation: how reproductive isolation arises and how it is measured
docs.excerpt: Two lineages become separate species when the barriers to gene exchange between them accumulate. Each barrier can be measured — and genomic data have shown that most of them leak for far longer than the textbook account allowed.

docs.title: What experimental evolution can show: watching selection instead of inferring it
docs.excerpt: Most evolutionary inference is retrospective. In organisms with short generations and large populations, selection can be run forward under controlled conditions — which turns a historical argument into an experiment, within limits worth stating.

docs.title: Antimicrobial resistance: the mechanisms, the surveillance and what the burden numbers rest on
docs.excerpt: Resistance mechanisms are well characterised and mobile between species. The harder question is measurement — what surveillance systems actually count, and which modelling assumptions sit behind the global death estimates.

docs.title: Bacteria and archaea: two domains that look alike and are not
docs.excerpt: Archaea were classed as bacteria until ribosomal RNA said otherwise. The differences run through membrane stereochemistry, cell wall polymers and transcription machinery — none of which a microscope can see.

docs.title: Studying microbes: why the method decides what you find
docs.excerpt: A plate, a PCR primer and a metagenome assembler each return a different subset of the same community. This page sets out what every major microbiological method selects for, and the quality standards that make a genome without an organism reportable.

docs.title: Fungi: a kingdom closer to animals than to plants
docs.excerpt: Fungi feed by secreting enzymes and absorbing what dissolves, a body plan that makes them the main decomposers of wood and the hardest pathogens to design drugs against. Around 120,000 species are described against an estimate of 2.2 to 3.8 million.

docs.title: Microbial biogeochemistry: the organisms that close the elemental cycles
docs.excerpt: Several steps in the nitrogen, carbon and sulfur cycles have no plant or animal equivalent — only prokaryotes run them. This page follows those reactions and the awkward distance between detecting the gene for one and measuring its rate.

docs.title: Microbial energy limits: life at a millionth of a laboratory power budget
docs.excerpt: Cells in deep marine sediment subsist on power measured in tenths of an attowatt — a millionth of what a starving laboratory culture uses. The measurements move dormancy from a curiosity to the ordinary state of most cells on Earth.

docs.title: Microbiology: the organisms that run the planet's chemistry
docs.excerpt: Bacteria alone hold about 70 gigatonnes of carbon, most of it in the deep subsurface, and microbes run reactions no plant or animal can. This page sets out what has been counted, what is inferred, and where the field's numbers remain unsettled.

docs.title: Microbiomes: what sequencing surveys can and cannot establish
docs.excerpt: A microbiome survey reports proportions at a total the sequencer chose, not a census of a gut. This page separates what that data structure can support from the causal claims that require a transplant, a gnotobiotic host, or a trial.

docs.title: Mycorrhizal symbiosis and nutrient uptake: renting a root system for a fifth of the sugar
docs.excerpt: Plants trade up to a fifth of their fixed carbon for phosphate delivered by fungi, and in some species the fungal route supplies all of it. The reason is a depletion zone that roots create around themselves and cannot grow out of fast enough.

docs.title: Nitrogen fixation and its cost: sixteen ATP, and an enzyme that oxygen destroys
docs.excerpt: Nitrogenase reduces one molecule of nitrogen at the cost of sixteen ATP and eight electrons, and releases hydrogen it did not need to make. It is also destroyed by oxygen, which is why the symbiosis that uses it is built the way it is.

docs.title: The limits of chemical sensing: how well a cell can measure a concentration
docs.excerpt: Berg and Purcell calculated in 1977 the best precision any cell can achieve when measuring a concentration by counting molecules. The bound depends on size, diffusion and time — and bacteria operate close to it.

docs.title: Viruses: replication strategies and the question of whether they are alive
docs.excerpt: Every virus faces the same problem — producing messenger RNA a host ribosome will read. The seven routes to that outcome organise virology better than shape or host does, and they explain why some viruses evolve past a vaccine and others do not.

docs.title: Circulation: pressure, flow and the price of a closed system
docs.excerpt: A circulatory system is a set of bills — pressure to be generated, gravity to be beaten, fluid to be kept inside the vessels. Reading vertebrate and invertebrate designs as different ways of paying them explains more than ranking them does.

docs.title: Development: how one cell becomes a patterned organism
docs.excerpt: Every cell in an embryo carries the same genome, so development is not a question of what the instructions say but of how a cell learns where it is. Gradients, screens and transplants are how that question was made experimental.

docs.title: Diffusion limits on body size: why anything bigger than a millimetre needs plumbing
docs.excerpt: Oxygen reaches a cell by diffusion, and diffusion is fast only over very short distances. That single physical fact sets a ceiling on how large an animal can be without a circulatory system, and explains what circulation is actually for.

docs.title: Heat stress and thermoregulatory limits: four reasons the body fails before the physics does
docs.excerpt: An idealised body loses heat until the air is as warm and wet as its skin. A real one stops sooner, because its skin is warmer than the model assumes, its sweat rate is regulated, its clothing gets in the way, and it may not be acclimatised.

docs.title: Endocrine signalling: slow, broadcast, and amplified
docs.excerpt: A hormone carries no address. It reaches every tissue the blood reaches, and the specificity lives entirely in which cells hold a receptor — which is why solubility, amplification and timing decide what an endocrine signal can do.

docs.title: Metabolic scaling and body size: the exponent that stopped being three quarters
docs.excerpt: Kleiber's quarter-power law was treated as one of biology's few quantitative universals for seventy years. A reanalysis of 619 mammal species found an exponent of about two thirds instead, and the disagreement is about method rather than about mammals.

docs.title: Neurons and nervous systems: signalling by controlled ion leaks
docs.excerpt: A neuron spends energy building an ion gradient so that it can discharge part of it on demand. That arrangement explains the all-or-nothing spike, the value of myelin, and what a brain scan is actually measuring.

docs.title: Physiology: how organisms hold conditions steady while everything changes
docs.excerpt: Regulation is not a thermostat. This pillar sets out what a regulated variable is, why the set point is a modelling convenience rather than a number in the body, and how size and species decide which design an organism can afford.

docs.title: Plant physiology: moving water without a pump
docs.excerpt: A tree raises water tens of metres with no moving part, using evaporation to put the column under tension. That solution explains stomatal behaviour, embolism risk and why forests everywhere run close to a hydraulic limit.

docs.title: Gas exchange: surface area, gradients and the countercurrent solution
docs.excerpt: Oxygen crosses the last few micrometres into blood by diffusion alone, so every breathing organ is an answer to the same equation. The variables are area, distance and partial-pressure difference — and flow geometry decides how much of the gradient survives.

docs.title: Temperature and biological rates: what the 0.65 eV constant is, and how much it varies
docs.excerpt: Biological rates rise with temperature in a way that looks Arrhenius-like, and a single activation energy near 0.65 eV is widely used to summarise it. A survey of 1,072 thermal responses found that mean holds and that the variation around it is systematic.

docs.title: Immunity: a layered system, not a single defence
docs.excerpt: An immune system has to recognise pathogens that have not evolved yet. Vertebrates solve that by manufacturing receptor diversity at random, then editing it — and plants and invertebrates show the problem has other solutions.

docs.title: Thermoregulation: the energetics of holding a temperature
docs.excerpt: Body temperature is not defended by a thermostat but by an energy budget with five terms. Reading that budget explains why endothermy costs what it does, why hibernation exists, and why the famous 35 °C wet-bulb limit turned out to be too generous.

docs.title: Plant diversity: the major lineages and what each innovation solved
docs.excerpt: Land plants descend from one lineage of freshwater green algae, and their major groups mark successive solutions to drying out, standing upright, and reproducing without free water. The counts across those groups are wildly unequal.

docs.title: DNA barcoding and its limits: 97 per cent for old species, 75 for young ones
docs.excerpt: A short standard sequence identifies most specimens to species, and its failures are not random. Success falls from about 97 per cent for older species to about 75 per cent for recently diverged ones, which is exactly where identification matters most.

docs.title: Environmental DNA and what it detects: a negative result is mostly a statement about volume
docs.excerpt: At low target concentrations, eDNA surveys miss species that are present, and simulation shows why: at 10 copies per litre, 97 per cent of PCR replicates contain nothing at all. Increasing sample volume helps more than increasing replicates.

docs.title: How many species exist: the estimate depends entirely on the method
docs.excerpt: Catalogues of life hold roughly 2.2 million named species, while published estimates of the true total run from a few million to a trillion. That gap is not measurement error — it is what happens when incompatible methods answer the same question.

docs.title: Molecular clocks and divergence dating: why more sequence data does not narrow the date
docs.excerpt: Divergence times are estimated by combining sequence differences with fossil calibrations, and the two quantities the method must separate are confounded. Adding sequence has a limit that adding loci does not.

docs.title: Phylogenetics: reconstructing history from present-day data
docs.excerpt: A phylogenetic tree is an estimate produced by a model from living molecules, and every figure attached to it describes the estimate rather than the past. Here is where the errors enter and what the support values really measure.

docs.title: Taxonomy: naming, ranking, and the rules that keep names stable
docs.excerpt: Naming an organism is a rule-governed procedure with its own codes, types and priority rules, and it is separate from the scientific judgement about which organisms belong together. This is how that machinery works and where it strains.

docs.title: The tree of life: three domains, two domains, and a network
docs.excerpt: Ribosomal RNA split the prokaryotes in two in 1977 and gave biology its three domains. Asgard archaea, endosymbiosis and gene transfer have since turned the deepest part of that diagram into an argument that is still open.

docs.title: The species problem: a working concept that no definition fully captures
docs.excerpt: Biologists apply at least five incompatible criteria for deciding where one kind of organism ends and the next begins. The disagreements are rarely about the data, and they propagate straight into conservation counts.

docs.title: Animal diversity: body plans, and what the phylogenomic revision changed
docs.excerpt: Molecular data reorganised the animal tree in the 1990s and phylogenomics has been revising it ever since. What changed was not the list of phyla but which of them are relatives — and the position of the root is still open.

docs.title: Bioinformatics: four inferences between the sequencer and the result
docs.excerpt: Sequence data becomes a finding only after alignment, assembly, annotation and statistical filtering have each made an inference. This page follows those four steps and the characteristic way each one fails.

docs.title: Biotechnology: what the techniques do, and where the claims outrun them
docs.excerpt: Recombinant DNA, sequencing, editing and computational design each made one thing cheap and left the hard parts untouched. This is what the toolkit does, how a laboratory result becomes a product, and where that path breaks.

docs.title: Agricultural biotechnology: what the evidence resolves and what it leaves open
docs.excerpt: Two traits account for most of the engineered crop area, the food-safety literature is large and consistent, and the agronomic failures were the ones evolutionary theory predicted. The open questions are about distribution and management, not toxicity.

docs.title: CRISPR: the bacterial immune system that became an editing tool
docs.excerpt: A guided nuclease cuts DNA; the cell decides what the cut becomes. That division of labour explains why knockouts are routine, precise replacements are hard, and delivery — not targeting — is the limiting step.

docs.title: Sequencing technologies: read length, error profile, and what each is good for
docs.excerpt: Choosing a sequencing platform is less about headline accuracy than about the shape of its errors and the length of its reads. Here is how the main families differ, why depth requirements vary, and what the cost curve leaves out.

docs.title: Metagenome-assembled genomes and their quality: what a MAG is allowed to be missing
docs.excerpt: A genome reconstructed from a mixed community is a statistical assembly, not an isolate. The MIMAG standard says how incomplete and how contaminated it may be and still be called high quality — 90 per cent and 5 per cent respectively.

docs.title: Protein structure prediction: a benchmark largely won, and the residue it left
docs.excerpt: Deep-learning models closed most of the gap between sequence and fold on the blind CASP targets. What remains — assemblies, disorder, alternative conformations, mutation effects — is where the difficulty moved rather than where it ended.

docs.title: Reference materials in genome measurement: how a sequencing result is checked
docs.excerpt: A genome sequence has no SI unit and no calibration standard. What it has instead is a small set of human genomes characterised so thoroughly that they can be used as a ruler, which is a different kind of metrology and a harder one.

docs.title: Synthetic biology: engineering principles meeting biological variability
docs.excerpt: The field was founded on an analogy with electronics — standard parts, datasheets, predictable composition. The parts exist. What has proved harder is that the host keeps changing the circuit while it runs.

docs.title: Battery energy density and its limits: 299 Wh/kg, and what it would take to beat it
docs.excerpt: Lithium-ion batteries with graphite anodes are near their ceiling at around 299 Wh per kilogram. Lithium metal offers ten times graphite's capacity and would roughly double the pack, and four failure modes have kept it out of production for decades.

docs.title: Reading energy statistics: capacity factor, LCOE, and the metrics that mislead
docs.excerpt: Nameplate capacity, capacity factor, levelised cost and primary energy are four different accounts of the same fleet, and each carries a convention that can move a headline without anything physical changing.

docs.title: Cooling demand and electricity: the load that arrives when the grid is weakest
docs.excerpt: Air conditioning demand rises steeply with temperature — around 1 to 9 per cent for every 2 °F in US cities — and it peaks at the hours when thermal generation and transmission are least capable. The coincidence is the problem, not the total.

docs.title: Critical minerals and supply concentration: the bottleneck is refining, not mining
docs.excerpt: The share of critical mineral refining held by the top three countries rose to 86 per cent in 2024, up from around 82 per cent in 2020. Concentration is increasing while investment growth is slowing, and the constraint sits in processing rather than in the ground.

docs.title: Energy storage: the quantities that matter are duration and energy, not power
docs.excerpt: A store advertised in megawatts has told you how fast it can move energy and nothing about how much it holds. This page separates power, energy and duration, then works through round-trip losses and the chemistry of capacity fade.

docs.title: Energy systems: conversion, carriers, and the constraints that decide what scales
docs.excerpt: Primary energy, energy carriers and final consumption are three separate accounts, and mixing them produces most bad energy arguments. This page follows the conversion chain from resource to end use and names where the losses and the limits actually sit.

docs.title: Grid integration: what variability actually costs a power system
docs.excerpt: The cost of wind and solar in a power system is mostly not a cost of energy. It is the price of frequency control, curtailment, firm capacity and wires — four separate problems that get collapsed into one word.

docs.title: Hydrogen: an energy carrier with an efficiency penalty at every step
docs.excerpt: A kilogram of hydrogen holds 33.3 kWh and costs roughly 50 to 64 kWh of electricity to make. Every later step — compression, storage, transport, reconversion — takes another cut, and that arithmetic decides where hydrogen belongs.

docs.title: Life-cycle emissions and how they are compared: what a single number per kilowatt-hour contains
docs.excerpt: Comparing generation technologies on grams of CO2 per kilowatt-hour requires deciding what to include, and the decision is where most of the disagreement lives. Published compilations report quartiles rather than point values for exactly that reason.

docs.title: Perovskite tandem cells: closing the gap between lab efficiency and outdoor reality
docs.excerpt: Encapsulation, ion-migration suppression, and tandem architectures are narrowing the gap between high laboratory efficiency and durable outdoor performance.

docs.title: Recycling and material circularity: a quarter to two-fifths off the growth in mining
docs.excerpt: Scaling up recycling could cut the growth in new mining supply for critical minerals by 25 to 40 per cent by mid-century. That is a large reduction in growth and not the same thing as a closed loop, and the difference is arithmetic rather than ambition.

docs.title: Photovoltaics: from photon absorption to a rated module
docs.excerpt: A module's nameplate wattage is a measurement made against a modelled spectrum at a fixed temperature, not a prediction of field output. This page follows the physics from photon absorption to the rating, and then to what the rating omits.

docs.title: Solar radiation and Earth's energy balance: the physics behind the climate
docs.excerpt: The Earth absorbs a specific amount of energy from the Sun and radiates a specific amount back to space. The accounting between the two is the foundation of climate physics.

docs.title: The energy cost of ammonia synthesis: two per cent of world energy for one molecule
docs.excerpt: Breaking the nitrogen triple bond industrially takes around two per cent of global final energy and produces 1.3 per cent of energy-system CO2. Roughly 70 per cent of the output becomes fertiliser, which makes this an agricultural number as much as an industrial one.

docs.title: Wind energy: cubic scaling, the Betz limit, and why turbines got large
docs.excerpt: Power in the wind rises with the cube of speed, which makes a resource assessment a measurement problem before it is an engineering one. This page derives the extraction ceiling and follows the scaling arguments that drove turbine size.

docs.title: Earth's climate is a heat engine: thermodynamics and the planetary energy budget
docs.excerpt: A planet receives concentrated radiation from a hot source, redistributes it, and emits it back to space at a colder temperature. This is a heat engine. The thermodynamics is what bounds the climate.

docs.title: Entropy: what the quantity measures, and where the analogies break
docs.excerpt: Entropy was defined as a ratio of heat to temperature before anyone knew what it counted. The statistical reading came later and connects to the first through a constant the SI now fixes exactly.

docs.title: Free energy and biological work: what a cell can actually buy with a molecule
docs.excerpt: The textbook figure for ATP hydrolysis is a standard-state value that no cell ever experiences. The number that governs what a cell can do is larger, it depends on concentrations the cell holds far from equilibrium, and the difference is the whole point.

docs.title: Heat engines: the Carnot ceiling and where the missing efficiency goes
docs.excerpt: A coal steam plant converts about a third of its fuel energy to electricity against a reversible ceiling near two thirds. The gap is mostly deliberate, and the reasons are temperature limits, finite-rate operation and where the accounting boundary is drawn.

docs.title: Heat transfer: three mechanisms that scale differently with temperature
docs.excerpt: Conduction and convection rise roughly in step with a temperature difference; radiation rises as the fourth power of absolute temperature. That difference in exponent decides which mechanism dominates, and it changes with the working temperature.

docs.title: Information and thermodynamics: what erasing a bit costs, and why it is not zero
docs.excerpt: Landauer argued in 1961 that discarding a bit must dissipate at least kT ln 2 of heat. The bound is tiny, it took fifty years to measure, and it is the reason Maxwell's demon does not work.

docs.title: The laws of thermodynamics: what each one actually forbids
docs.excerpt: The four laws are prohibitions, not recipes. Each one rules out a class of machine or process, and together they fix what temperature means, what energy accounting must balance, and which direction a process can run.

docs.title: The kelvin and the Boltzmann constant: a unit that stopped depending on water
docs.excerpt: For 64 years the kelvin was defined as a fraction of the triple-point temperature of water. Since 2019 it is defined by fixing the Boltzmann constant, and the change matters most where the old definition was weakest — very high and very low temperatures.

docs.title: The thermodynamic limits of photovoltaics — and why they matter for what's possible
docs.excerpt: There is a hard upper bound on how much sunlight any single-junction photovoltaic cell can convert to electricity. Knowing where it comes from clarifies which directions of improvement are physics, and which are engineering.

docs.title: Atomic clocks and the second: counting 9,192,631,770 oscillations
docs.excerpt: The second is defined by counting a fixed number of microwave oscillations in caesium. Commercial caesium clocks keep time to within a third of a microsecond a year, and experimental clocks on other atoms are ten thousand times better.

docs.title: The electromagnetic spectrum: one phenomenon, many windows on the universe
docs.excerpt: Radio waves, visible light, X-rays, and gamma rays are not different phenomena. They are the same phenomenon at different wavelengths — and the wavelength determines what the radiation can do.

docs.title: Quantum computing: qubits, error rates, and the distance to useful machines
docs.excerpt: A 2025 surface-code result held one logical qubit on 101 physical qubits at 0.143 per cent error per cycle. Reading that number correctly explains both why the field is real and why the distance to a useful machine is measured in orders of magnitude.

docs.title: Quantum mechanics: the working rules, without the philosophy
docs.excerpt: Quantum theory pins physical constants to ten significant figures while its interpretation stays open. This page sets out the working rules — amplitudes, observables, quantisation, uncertainty, spin statistics, decoherence — and marks where the real gaps sit.

docs.title: Wave-particle duality: what the experiments actually show
docs.excerpt: Nothing switches between being a wave and being a particle. Interference builds up one detection at a time, the de Broglie wavelength of a baseball is 10⁻³⁴ m, and which-path information destroys fringes for a reason that is not momentum kicks.

docs.title: Why wavelength decides what radiation does: one spectrum, several biologies
docs.excerpt: Radio waves and gamma rays are the same phenomenon, and what each does to matter is set by photon energy alone. Following that single variable across the spectrum explains why 5 per cent of ultraviolet does most of the DNA damage and why visible light drives photosynthesis.

docs.title: Atmospheric physics: the machine that moves energy from equator to pole
docs.excerpt: The atmosphere holds about ten tonnes of air over every square metre and its poleward energy transport peaks near five petawatts. This page sets out the composition, vertical structure, energy budget and transport mechanics the rest of the subject rests on.

docs.title: Lapse rates and stability: why the troposphere convects and the stratosphere does not
docs.excerpt: Two different quantities are both called the lapse rate, and confusing them produces most of the errors made about atmospheric stability. Here is what each one measures, how they combine, and what the tropopause definition actually says.

docs.title: Cloud physics: from a condensation nucleus to the widest uncertainty in climate sensitivity
docs.excerpt: Clouds cool the present-day planet by roughly 20 W/m², and their response to warming is still the largest single source of spread in climate sensitivity. Those two statements are not in tension, and understanding why is most of the subject.

docs.title: Geophysics: how the inside of the Earth is known without ever reaching it
docs.excerpt: No instrument has been inside the mantle. The layered picture of Earth's interior is assembled from waves that pass through it, heat that leaks out of it, a magnetic field it generates and a gravity field that satellites weigh from orbit.

docs.title: Humidity and why heat and moisture combine: the physics behind a heat index
docs.excerpt: Air temperature alone does not say how hot a place is to be in, because the last route for shedding heat is evaporation and evaporation depends on the vapour gradient. Every combined index is an attempt to state that in one number, and every one hides its assumptions.

docs.title: The greenhouse effect: the emission-height argument, done properly
docs.excerpt: Neither the blanket nor the greenhouse describes what actually happens. The mechanism is a shift in the altitude from which the planet radiates to space, and it only works because temperature falls with height.

docs.title: Calibration and traceability: what it means for a number to be defensible
docs.excerpt: A measurement is comparable to another only if both can be traced, through an unbroken chain of calibrations with stated uncertainties, to the same reference. That chain is infrastructure, and most disputes about data are really disputes about it.

docs.title: Classical mechanics: the framework that still describes most of the world
docs.excerpt: Newton's laws are less a set of facts about objects than a contract about reference frames and force laws. This page states that contract carefully, shows why the conservation principles turned out to be deeper, and marks the edges of the domain.

docs.title: Work, energy and power: the definitions that most confusion comes from
docs.excerpt: Almost every argument about energy is really a disagreement about definitions. Work is a path integral, power is a rate, and only some of the familiar unit conversions are exact — the rest are empirical averages that are revised each year.

docs.title: Fluid dynamics: why one dimensionless number decides how a flow behaves
docs.excerpt: A swimming ciliate and a hurricane obey the same equations. What separates them is the ratio of inertia to viscosity, and that ratio decides whether a flow is smooth, chaotic, or beyond the reach of direct calculation.

docs.title: Interlaboratory comparison and consensus values: measuring without a standard
docs.excerpt: When no certified material exists, the reference value is whatever independent laboratories agree on. That is a workable substitute with a specific failure mode, and the failure mode is shared method rather than shared error.

docs.title: Life at low Reynolds number: why a bacterium cannot coast
docs.excerpt: Below a Reynolds number of about one, inertia is irrelevant and a swimmer that repeats its motion in reverse returns exactly where it started. That constraint — Purcell's scallop theorem — determines what shapes of propulsion are available to anything small.

docs.title: Measurement uncertainty: what a stated ± actually claims
docs.excerpt: A number without an uncertainty is not a measurement result. This is what the international guidance asks of an interval, how the components are evaluated and combined, and the places where an uncertainty budget quietly fails.

docs.title: Optics: reflection, refraction, diffraction and the limits of an image
