docs.excerpt: Ray optics is an approximation that works until the aperture gets small, and then diffraction sets a floor no amount of engineering removes. This page traces that boundary through lenses, fibres, thin films, telescopes and polarimetry.

docs.title: The SI and its defining constants: seven numbers, fixed by decision
docs.excerpt: Since 2019 every SI unit is derived from seven constants whose numerical values are exact by definition. Nothing about nature changed; what changed is which quantities carry the uncertainty.

docs.title: Transport by diffusion and by flow: the crossover that organises biology and the ocean
docs.excerpt: Diffusion beats flow at small scales and loses badly at large ones, and the crossover falls at a distance you can state. Where a system sits relative to it explains cell size, capillary spacing, and why the ocean needs to be stirred.

docs.title: What changed when the kilogram changed: from a cylinder to a constant
docs.excerpt: For more than a century the kilogram was a platinum-iridium cylinder cast in 1879, and the copies of it drifted apart. Redefining it through the Planck constant removed the one unit whose value depended on an object nobody could check against anything.

docs.title: Atoms and nuclei: the single curve behind fission and fusion
docs.excerpt: An atom and the nucleus at its centre differ by four orders of magnitude in size and six in energy. That gap is why chemistry and nuclear physics behave as separate subjects, and why one binding-energy curve governs both fission and fusion.

docs.title: Counting atoms and the mole: a unit that stopped being about carbon
docs.excerpt: The mole used to be defined by a mass of carbon-12; it is now defined as a number. That severs chemistry's counting unit from mass, and the separation is the point rather than a side effect.

docs.title: Ionising radiation and risk: what the epidemiology can and cannot settle
docs.excerpt: Above a few hundred millisieverts the health effects of ionising radiation are directly observed. Below that, estimates come from extrapolation — and the shape of that extrapolation is a live scientific argument with real consequences.

docs.title: Materials for magnets, and why substitution is hard
docs.excerpt: Rare earth elements are in wind turbine generators and electric motors because of a property that comes from their electronic structure. That is why substituting them is a different kind of problem from substituting a battery chemistry.

docs.title: Band structure: why a few electron-volts decide whether a solid conducts
docs.excerpt: What separates copper from quartz is not how many electrons a material has but whether an energy gap sits between the states they occupy and the states they could move in. Almost every modern device is engineering on that gap.

docs.title: Becquerel, gray, sievert: three units that answer three different questions
docs.excerpt: A count of decays, an energy deposit and a risk-weighted estimate are not interchangeable, yet radiation reporting swaps them routinely. Here is what each unit in the chain measures, and the point at which each one stops meaning anything.

docs.title: Ocean circulation and climate: two circulations, two timescales, one heat pump
docs.excerpt: Wind drives the ocean's surface; density drives its interior. Which one you mean determines whether the relevant timescale is a season or a millennium.

docs.title: Food webs and trophic structure: what a trophic level actually counts
docs.excerpt: A trophic level is an accounting device for energy flow, not a category of organism. What the ten per cent rule really claims, why omnivory makes levels fractional, and how contested the Yellowstone case still is.

docs.title: Fragmentation, connectivity, and the corridor evidence
docs.excerpt: Habitat loss and fragmentation per se are separate variables, and holding one constant while varying the other reverses several familiar conclusions. Here is the global picture, the live disagreement, and what the corridor experiments show.

docs.title: The marine plastic budget: inputs, surface stocks, and the mass that appeared to go missing
docs.excerpt: For a decade the estimated flow of plastic into the sea exceeded the mass measured floating on it by one to two orders of magnitude. Tracing how that discrepancy was investigated is the clearest route into what marine debris research can and cannot measure.

docs.title: Rivers: the flow regime as the master variable
docs.excerpt: A streamgage records water level, not water. Everything ecologists say about river flow at large scales is a rating curve applied to a height — and five properties of that flow, not the annual average, organise river ecology.

docs.title: Water quality: the standard parameters, and what routine monitoring cannot see
docs.excerpt: Water quality is not a property of water but a comparison between a measurement and a purpose. What the routine physical, chemical and biological parameters record, how a legal threshold is built, and which failures the apparatus is poor at detecting.

docs.title: Heavy metals in the environment: the element is not the exposure
docs.excerpt: A total-metal concentration is rarely the quantity that decides harm. For arsenic, mercury, lead and cadmium the chemical form governs uptake and toxicity, and in the case of mercury the dangerous form is manufactured in the environment itself.

docs.title: Persistent organic pollutants: the four screening tests that put a chemical on a treaty list
docs.excerpt: A persistent organic pollutant is defined by four measurable properties written into treaty text, not by chemical family. Those tests explain Arctic contamination, and they are also where PFAS strain the definition.

docs.title: Natural selection: the conditions, the modes, and how adaptation is tested
docs.excerpt: Natural selection follows from three conditions that can be checked one at a time. The harder problem is showing that a given trait is an adaptation at all, and measured selection in the wild turns out to be weaker than most accounts imply.

docs.title: Global circulation: why the trade winds blow from the east
docs.excerpt: A non-rotating planet would carry air from equator to pole in one cell and give every surface wind a poleward heading. Rotation replaces that with three cells, two jet streams, easterly trades, and a tropical belt that is measurably widening.

docs.title: Inside a climate model: what is solved, what is parameterised, and what tuning can reach
docs.excerpt: A climate model is two pieces of software bolted together — a solver for equations that are known exactly, and a library of approximations for everything smaller than a grid cell. Nearly every contested result lives in the second half.

docs.title: Radiative transfer: absorption, emission, and why the spectrum matters more than the total
docs.excerpt: Radiative transfer is bookkeeping done wavelength by wavelength. A temperature fixes what a body emits, molecular structure fixes what the air absorbs, and almost every interesting result comes from the mismatch between the two.

docs.title: Sound and acoustics: a decibel is a ratio, and half the number is the reference
docs.excerpt: Sound is a pressure fluctuation travelling through a compressible medium. Almost every misreading of an acoustic figure comes from forgetting that a decibel is a logarithm of a ratio, and that the ratio needs a stated reference.

docs.title: Waves and oscillations: one mathematics, many physical systems
docs.excerpt: A pendulum, a quartz crystal, a swaying footbridge and a tsunami obey the same small set of equations. This page follows that mathematics from the simple oscillator to dispersion, and stops at the point where the shared model stops working.

docs.title: Fission reactors: the neutron budget and the heat that does not switch off
docs.excerpt: A fission does not release all its energy at once. That single fact — a delayed remainder arriving over hours and years — shapes reactor control, shutdown cooling and spent-fuel handling more than any other feature of the physics.

docs.title: Fusion: three conditions at once, and the distance still to go
docs.excerpt: Fusion needs temperature, density and confinement time together, and no device has yet held all three long enough to run. This separates the physics from the engineering, and scientific gain from net electricity.

docs.title: The Standard Model: what it accounts for, and the 95% it does not
docs.excerpt: Twelve matter particles and four force carriers describe every laboratory measurement made so far. They also describe about five per cent of the universe, and the theory says nothing about the rest.

docs.title: The Red List Index explained: tracking extinction risk over time
docs.excerpt: The IUCN Red List sorts species into extinction-risk categories; the Red List Index turns repeated assessments into a trend. Here is how the categories and criteria work, what the index does to avoid measuring its own improving knowledge, and which groups it can represent.

docs.title: The Copernicus programme explained: Europe’s Earth-observation system
docs.excerpt: Copernicus is the European Union’s Earth-observation programme, pairing the Sentinel satellites with six thematic services and a full, free, and open data policy. This explains how it is organised, who runs each service, and what it delivers.

docs.title: Earth observation data products: from raw signal to analysis-ready data
docs.excerpt: A number recorded by a satellite is not yet science. This explains the processing levels that turn raw instrument data into geophysical measurements, what analysis-ready and surface-reflectance products are, and where the major open archives live.

docs.title: The Landsat program explained: the longest continuous view of the land
docs.excerpt: Since 1972 the joint NASA–USGS Landsat satellites have built the longest unbroken record of Earth’s land surface. This explains the mission history, the 30-metre sensors, the free-data policy, and why a multi-decade archive is so scientifically valuable.

docs.title: NDVI explained: the vegetation index read from red and near-infrared light
docs.excerpt: NDVI is the most widely used satellite vegetation index, built from the contrast between the red light plants absorb and the near-infrared they reflect. This explains the formula, the −1 to +1 range, what the values mean, and where the index breaks down.

docs.title: Remote-sensing limitations and uncertainty: reading satellite data honestly
docs.excerpt: Satellite data are powerful but never perfect. This sets out the structural limits of remote sensing — resolution trade-offs, cloud, mixed pixels, indirect measurement, and sensor drift — and the validation practices that keep satellite products honest.

docs.title: Satellite altimetry explained: measuring sea level from orbit
docs.excerpt: Radar altimeters measure the height of the sea surface to within centimetres by timing a pulse to the water and back. This explains how altimetry works, the reference missions since 1992, what it measures beyond sea level, and the corrections it depends on.

docs.title: Vegetation indices and monitoring: beyond NDVI
docs.excerpt: NDVI is the best known vegetation index but not the only one. This explains why several indices exist — EVI, soil- and water-adjusted indices — what limitation each one corrects, and how index time series are used to monitor vegetation condition and productivity.

docs.title: Wildfire monitoring from space: active fires and burned area
docs.excerpt: Satellites detect wildfires in two ways — spotting the heat of active flames and mapping the scar they leave behind. This explains the thermal and reflectance methods, the near-real-time systems built on them, and why some fires are still missed from orbit.

docs.title: Why "AI for science" is undervaluing the bottleneck it is best placed to fix
docs.excerpt: Most AI-for-science investment chases discovery. The higher-leverage use is making the experimental record reproducible and machine-readable.

docs.title: Carbon offset markets are quietly outsourcing the work of climate science
docs.excerpt: Voluntary carbon markets have become the largest unregulated funder of forest-carbon measurement — and the methods are diverging from what the science actually says.

docs.title: What a biodiversity index can carry, and where it is asked to carry too much
docs.excerpt: The Living Planet Index, the Red List Index, species richness and protected-area coverage each aggregate a different quantity over a differently biased sample, and each supports a narrower claim than the way it is usually quoted.

docs.title: Not all climate-projection uncertainty is the same kind, and only one kind answers to better models
docs.excerpt: Scenario choice, model response and internal variability contribute to projection spread in proportions that shift with lead time and spatial scale. Only one of the three is a modelling problem, and it has not narrowed.

docs.title: Sorting energy-transition constraints into the ones physics imposes and the ones we do
docs.excerpt: Some limits on energy technology follow from conservation laws and cannot be negotiated. Others are administrative arrangements described in the same tone of voice. The diagnostic that separates them is simple, and it matters.

docs.title: The observation base for environmental science is contracting where it is least replaceable
docs.excerpt: Station counts can stay flat while the long records inside them disappear. A broken multi-decadal series cannot be reconstructed afterwards, and satellites supplement in-situ measurement rather than replacing it.

docs.title: A nature-based solution is a policy category, not a single body of evidence
docs.excerpt: The label covers interventions the IPCC grades from robust to limited evidence. Bundling them lets the best-measured members lend credibility to the least-measured, which is a problem of accounting rather than of ecology.

docs.title: Uncertainty is not lost gradually; it is dropped at one identifiable step
docs.excerpt: Environmental numbers carry explicit qualifiers through the instrument, the dataset and the assessment, then lose them in a single act of compression. The qualifier that vanishes is almost always a probability, a period or a baseline.

docs.title: The limits of Earth observation are systematic, not random
docs.excerpt: Cloud, canopy, depth and orbit geometry put the same variables out of reach on every pass. A gap that falls in the same place each time does not average away as more observations accumulate.

docs.title: A disagreement between two good datasets is a fact about the products, not about the world
docs.excerpt: Authoritative sources routinely publish different values for the same environmental quantity. Five recurring causes account for nearly all of it, and each one can be identified from the source documentation in a few minutes.

docs.title: Whether adaptation can keep pace is an empirical question with partial answers
docs.excerpt: Plasticity, evolutionary change and range shift are three responses on three timescales, and the published evidence is strongest for the one that is easiest to observe and weakest for the one that would matter most.

docs.title: Event attribution answers a narrower question than the one it is usually quoted for
docs.excerpt: An attribution study estimates how much human influence changed the odds or the severity of a defined class of event. It cannot name the cause of one particular storm, and it cannot apportion the damage that followed.

docs.title: Every extinction-rate number is a model, and the models disagree about what they are counting
docs.excerpt: The claim that species are disappearing hundreds or thousands of times faster than normal is a ratio between two model outputs built from different taxa, different data types and different timescales. It inherits every assumption in both.

docs.title: Microbiome research produces associations far faster than it produces causes
docs.excerpt: Sequencing made microbial community composition cheap to measure and did nothing to make causation cheaper to establish. A systematic review found that 36 of 38 human-microbiota transfer studies in rodents reported a positive result.

docs.title: Ecology's reproducibility problem is real, and it is not a copy of psychology's
docs.excerpt: Surveys find questionable research practices in ecology at rates close to those in psychology, but an ecological field study usually cannot be re-run. That changes both how an unreliable literature is diagnosed and what fixes it.

docs.title: Restoration is judged on a timescale far shorter than the one it operates on
docs.excerpt: Half the published restoration record has ten years or less of observation, against processes that take decades. Most reported successes describe an early point on a trajectory whose end nobody has watched.

docs.title: Diurnal and seasonal storage are treated as one problem and are not
docs.excerpt: A store cycled every day and a store cycled twice a year are governed by different cost terms, and the technologies that won daily balancing are structurally poor candidates for multi-week duty.

docs.title: The soil-carbon signal is smaller than the sampling noise in a single field
docs.excerpt: Management adds carbon to farmland at roughly 0.2 to 0.8 tonnes per hectare a year, against a stock near 60 to 90 tonnes and a resampling error of 5 to 8. That ratio decides what a soil credit can honestly certify.

docs.title: Radiative forcing
docs.excerpt: The change in net radiative flux at the tropopause caused by a perturbation, measured in W/m².

docs.title: Greenhouse gas
docs.excerpt: An atmospheric gas that absorbs and re-emits infrared radiation in bands relevant to Earth's outgoing longwave.

docs.title: Ocean heat content
docs.excerpt: The integral of ocean temperature anomalies over a defined volume, typically reported in zettajoules.

docs.title: Carbon cycle
docs.excerpt: The flow of carbon among the atmosphere, ocean, biosphere, and geological reservoirs.

docs.title: Biodiversity indicator
docs.excerpt: A measurement used to track one dimension of biodiversity change over time.

docs.title: Ecosystem service
docs.excerpt: A benefit that people obtain from ecosystems, such as provisioning, regulating, cultural, or supporting functions.

docs.title: Climate attribution
docs.excerpt: Scientific assessment of how much a specific climate change or event is due to a given cause.

docs.title: Sea-level rise
docs.excerpt: The increase in global mean or local relative sea level, driven by thermal expansion and land-ice loss.

docs.title: Climate indicator
docs.excerpt: A measurement, sustained over time, that tracks one dimension of the Earth system with a known physical interpretation.

docs.title: Global mean surface temperature
docs.excerpt: Area-weighted average of near-surface air temperature over land and sea-surface temperature over ocean, reported as anomaly from a reference period.

docs.title: Cryosphere
docs.excerpt: The frozen components of the Earth system: sea ice, glaciers, ice sheets, snow cover, and permafrost.

docs.title: Carbon-cycle feedback
docs.excerpt: A change in the rate at which land or ocean absorbs anthropogenic CO₂ caused by the climate response to that CO₂.

docs.title: Climate projection
docs.excerpt: A model-based estimate of future climate statistics conditional on a specified forcing scenario.

docs.title: Detection and attribution
docs.excerpt: Statistical methodology that separates observed climate change into contributions from different forcing agents.

docs.title: Emissions scenario
docs.excerpt: A plausible trajectory of future greenhouse-gas emissions used as input to climate projections.

docs.title: Earth energy imbalance
docs.excerpt: The net difference between incoming solar shortwave radiation absorbed and outgoing longwave radiation emitted at the top of the atmosphere.

docs.title: Greenhouse-gas concentration
docs.excerpt: The atmospheric mole fraction of a greenhouse gas, typically reported in ppm (CO₂) or ppb (methane, nitrous oxide).

docs.title: Climate model
docs.excerpt: A numerical simulation of the climate system integrating the governing physical equations forward in time on a discrete grid.

docs.title: Glacier mass balance
docs.excerpt: The net gain or loss of ice mass on a glacier per year, typically reported in meters of water-equivalent.

docs.title: Species richness
docs.excerpt: The number of distinct species recorded in a defined area or sample — the simplest and most widely reported biodiversity measure.

docs.title: Species evenness
docs.excerpt: How equally individuals are distributed among the species in a community; combined with richness it determines diversity-index values.

docs.title: Red List Index
docs.excerpt: An indicator tracking the aggregate trend in extinction risk for a group of species, derived from repeated IUCN Red List assessments.

docs.title: Living Planet Index
docs.excerpt: An index of the average relative change in monitored vertebrate population sizes since 1970 — a measure of abundance, not a count of animals.

docs.title: Habitat fragmentation
docs.excerpt: The breaking of continuous habitat into smaller, more isolated patches; distinct from, though usually accompanying, habitat loss.

docs.title: Ecological integrity
docs.excerpt: The degree to which an ecosystem retains the species composition, structure, and function characteristic of its type, relative to a minimally disturbed reference.

docs.title: Ecosystem resilience
docs.excerpt: The capacity of an ecosystem to absorb disturbance and retain its essential structure and function rather than shifting to a different state.

docs.title: Baseline condition
docs.excerpt: The reference state against which biodiversity change is measured; the choice of baseline strongly shapes whether a system is judged degraded, stable, or recovering.

docs.title: Remote sensing
docs.excerpt: Measuring a surface from a distance by recording the electromagnetic radiation it reflects or emits — the basis of satellite Earth observation.

docs.title: Citizen science (biodiversity)
docs.excerpt: Biodiversity observations contributed by volunteers; aggregated through facilities such as GBIF, they greatly expand coverage but carry sampling biases.

docs.title: Protected-area effectiveness
docs.excerpt: Whether a protected area actually reduces the pressures and biodiversity loss it was created to address — distinct from how much area is designated.

docs.title: Earth observation
docs.excerpt: Gathering information about the planet's land, ocean, atmosphere, and ice using sensors on satellites and aircraft.

docs.title: Landsat
docs.excerpt: A joint NASA–USGS satellite program that has imaged Earth's land surface continuously since 1972 — the longest such record.

docs.title: Sentinel satellite
docs.excerpt: A satellite of the EU's Copernicus programme; the Sentinel families provide radar, optical, ocean, atmospheric, and altimetry data, free and open.

docs.title: MODIS
docs.excerpt: The Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer on NASA's Terra and Aqua satellites, imaging the whole planet almost daily.

docs.title: NDVI (Normalised Difference Vegetation Index)
docs.excerpt: A vegetation index, (NIR − Red)/(NIR + Red), ranging −1 to +1 — the most widely used satellite measure of vegetation greenness.

docs.title: Enhanced Vegetation Index (EVI)
docs.excerpt: A MODIS-standard vegetation index that improves on NDVI by reducing atmospheric and soil-background effects and resisting saturation at high biomass.

docs.title: Satellite altimetry
docs.excerpt: Measuring the height of a surface — usually the sea — by timing a radar pulse from a satellite and back; the basis of the satellite sea-level record.

docs.title: Land cover
docs.excerpt: The physical material covering the land surface — forest, water, cropland, built-up — as mapped from satellite imagery.

docs.title: Land-use change
docs.excerpt: A change in how people use land — for example forest converted to cropland — often inferred from satellite-detected land-cover change.

docs.title: Ocean colour
docs.excerpt: The spectrum of light leaving the sea surface, used to estimate chlorophyll and phytoplankton from space.

docs.title: Spectral signature
docs.excerpt: The characteristic way a material reflects or emits radiation across wavelengths, used to identify surfaces in remote sensing.

docs.title: Reflectance
docs.excerpt: The fraction of incoming radiation a surface reflects in a given wavelength band — the core quantity a calibrated optical sensor reports.

docs.title: Raster data
docs.excerpt: Spatial data stored as a grid of cells (pixels), each holding a value — the standard form of satellite imagery.

docs.title: Ground-truthing
docs.excerpt: Comparing a satellite estimate against independent field or higher-resolution observations to calibrate and validate it.

docs.title: Gene expression
docs.excerpt: The process by which information encoded in DNA is converted into functional product, typically protein.

docs.title: Cell signaling
docs.excerpt: The set of molecular mechanisms by which cells receive, process, and respond to signals from their environment.

docs.title: Antibiotic resistance
docs.excerpt: The evolved ability of a microorganism to survive an antibiotic that would otherwise inhibit or kill it.

docs.title: Microbiome
docs.excerpt: The community of microorganisms inhabiting a defined environment, together with their genetic material.

docs.title: Transcription
docs.excerpt: The synthesis of an RNA copy of a DNA template by RNA polymerase.

docs.title: Evolutionary adaptation
docs.excerpt: A heritable trait that has been shaped by natural selection because it improves fitness in a given environment.

docs.title: Energy balance
docs.excerpt: The accounting of energy entering, stored within, and leaving a defined system — Earth, in climate physics.

docs.title: Albedo
docs.excerpt: The fraction of incident shortwave radiation reflected by a surface or planet, dimensionless (0–1).

docs.title: Electromagnetic spectrum
docs.excerpt: The full range of electromagnetic radiation, ordered by wavelength or equivalently photon energy.

docs.title: Photon
docs.excerpt: The quantum of the electromagnetic field; the elementary excitation of light at a given frequency.

docs.title: Shockley–Queisser limit
docs.excerpt: The maximum theoretical efficiency of a single-junction solar cell under standard solar illumination — about 33%.

docs.title: Perovskite (solar materials)
docs.excerpt: A family of crystal structures (ABX₃) used in high-efficiency emerging photovoltaic devices.

docs.title: Earth system
docs.excerpt: The coupled whole formed by the atmosphere, hydrosphere, cryosphere, biosphere, and geosphere and the exchanges between them.

docs.title: Atmosphere
docs.excerpt: The gaseous envelope surrounding Earth — roughly 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen by volume, with trace gases doing most of the radiative work.

docs.title: Hydrosphere
docs.excerpt: All the water at and near Earth's surface — ocean, ice, fresh surface water, groundwater, and atmospheric moisture.

docs.title: Biosphere
docs.excerpt: The totality of living organisms and the zone they occupy, treated as an active component of the Earth system.

docs.title: Lithosphere
docs.excerpt: Earth's rigid outer rock shell — the crust and uppermost mantle — and, in Earth-system usage, the source of the slowest material cycles.

docs.title: Biogeochemical cycle
docs.excerpt: The movement of a chemical element between reservoirs by biological, geological, and chemical processes, described by reservoir sizes and fluxes.

docs.title: Residence time
docs.excerpt: The average time a unit of material stays in a reservoir — reservoir size divided by the total outgoing flux.

docs.title: Water cycle
docs.excerpt: The continuous circulation of water between ocean, atmosphere, land, and ice through evaporation, condensation, precipitation, and runoff.

docs.title: Nitrogen cycle
docs.excerpt: The transformation of nitrogen between inert atmospheric N2 and biologically reactive forms through fixation, nitrification, assimilation, and denitrification.

docs.title: Carbon sink
docs.excerpt: A reservoir that absorbs more carbon than it releases over a defined period; a carbon source does the reverse.

docs.title: Climate feedback
docs.excerpt: A process that changes Earth's energy budget in response to temperature change, quantified in watts per square metre per degree Celsius.

docs.title: Water-vapour feedback
docs.excerpt: The amplification of warming by the extra water vapour a warmer atmosphere holds, almost always assessed jointly with the lapse-rate feedback.

docs.title: Ice-albedo feedback
docs.excerpt: The amplification of warming that follows when retreating snow and ice expose darker, more absorptive surfaces.

docs.title: Ocean circulation
docs.excerpt: The organised movement of seawater — wind-driven at the surface, density-driven in the interior — that transports heat, salt, carbon, and nutrients.

docs.title: Thermohaline circulation
docs.excerpt: The deep, density-driven ocean overturning set by temperature and salinity, of which the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation is the best-studied component.

docs.title: ENSO (El Nino-Southern Oscillation)
docs.excerpt: The coupled ocean-atmosphere oscillation of the tropical Pacific, shifting irregularly between warm, cool, and neutral phases every two to seven years.

docs.title: El Nino
docs.excerpt: The warm phase of ENSO, in which trade winds relax, warm water spreads eastward, and eastern Pacific upwelling weakens.

docs.title: La Nina
docs.excerpt: The cool phase of ENSO, in which trade winds strengthen, the thermocline steepens, and eastern Pacific upwelling intensifies.

docs.title: Climate variability
docs.excerpt: Fluctuations arising from the internal dynamics of the coupled climate system rather than from an external change in forcing.

docs.title: Teleconnection
docs.excerpt: A statistical linkage between climate anomalies in widely separated regions, produced by large-scale atmospheric wave propagation rather than local transport.

docs.title: Earth system model
docs.excerpt: A coupled climate model extended with interactive biogeochemistry, so that atmospheric composition is computed rather than prescribed.

docs.title: Essential Climate Variable
docs.excerpt: One of the 55 variables GCOS specifies as critical for characterising the climate system and feasible to observe globally on a sustained basis.

docs.title: Tipping element
docs.excerpt: A component of the Earth system susceptible to a critical threshold beyond which it reorganises, often abruptly or irreversibly.

docs.title: Systematic conservation planning
docs.excerpt: A structured method for choosing conservation areas by complementarity and cost rather than by scenic or opportunistic criteria.

docs.title: Counterfactual (conservation evidence)
docs.excerpt: What would have happened to a site or population without the intervention — the comparison against which any conservation effect must be measured.

docs.title: Assisted migration
docs.excerpt: Deliberately moving a species outside its historical range to track shifting climate conditions.

docs.title: Genetic rescue
docs.excerpt: Introducing individuals from another population to restore genetic variation and reverse inbreeding depression in a small population.

docs.title: Trophic rewilding
docs.excerpt: Restoring ecological processes by reintroducing or substituting large animals, particularly predators and large herbivores.

docs.title: Reference state
docs.excerpt: The condition a restoration or assessment is measured against — the single choice that most determines whether a project is judged a success.

docs.title: Biological control
docs.excerpt: Managing a pest or invasive species by introducing or encouraging one of its natural enemies.

docs.title: Invasion stage
docs.excerpt: The point a non-native species has reached along the sequence transport, introduction, establishment, spread and impact.

docs.title: Area-based target
docs.excerpt: A conservation goal stated as a percentage of land or sea under protection, such as the 30 per cent target.

docs.title: Data Deficient
docs.excerpt: An IUCN Red List category meaning there is not enough information to assess extinction risk — not that the species is safe.

docs.title: Thermocline
docs.excerpt: The depth range over which ocean temperature falls steeply, separating the warm surface layer from the cold deep.

docs.title: Aragonite saturation state
docs.excerpt: A measure, written Ω, of whether seawater favours the formation or dissolution of aragonite, the calcium carbonate form used by corals and pteropods.

docs.title: Upwelling
docs.excerpt: Wind-driven rise of cold, nutrient-rich water from depth to the sunlit surface.

docs.title: Microbial loop
docs.excerpt: The pathway by which dissolved organic carbon is taken up by bacteria and returned to the food web through protist grazing.

docs.title: Degree heating week
docs.excerpt: An accumulated measure of heat stress on corals: the sum of weekly sea-surface temperatures above the local summer maximum, over twelve weeks.

docs.title: Chemosynthesis
docs.excerpt: Primary production powered by the oxidation of inorganic chemicals rather than by light.

docs.title: Maximum sustainable yield
docs.excerpt: The largest catch that can in theory be taken from a stock indefinitely.

docs.title: Spillover (marine reserves)
docs.excerpt: The movement of adults or larvae from a protected area into surrounding fished waters.

docs.title: Oxygen minimum zone
docs.excerpt: A mid-depth layer where dissolved oxygen falls to very low concentrations, formed where respiration consumes oxygen faster than circulation resupplies it.

docs.title: Missing plastic problem
docs.excerpt: The large gap between the amount of plastic estimated to enter the ocean and the amount measured floating at the surface.

docs.title: Natural flow regime
docs.excerpt: The characteristic pattern of a river’s flow described by magnitude, frequency, duration, timing and rate of change.

docs.title: Internal loading
docs.excerpt: The release of nutrients stored in lake sediments back into the water column, sustaining eutrophication after external inputs are cut.

docs.title: Thermal stratification (lakes)
docs.excerpt: The seasonal separation of a lake into a warm surface layer and a cold bottom layer, with a sharp density gradient between them.

docs.title: Aquifer recharge
docs.excerpt: The rate at which water percolates down to replenish groundwater.

docs.title: Land subsidence
docs.excerpt: Irreversible sinking of the ground surface as groundwater is removed and the aquifer compacts.

docs.title: Biotic index
docs.excerpt: A water-quality measure built from the composition of the resident invertebrate or algal community rather than from a chemical sample.

docs.title: Biochemical oxygen demand
docs.excerpt: The oxygen consumed by microorganisms decomposing organic matter in a water sample over a fixed period, usually five days.

docs.title: River connectivity
docs.excerpt: The extent to which a river remains continuous longitudinally, laterally to its floodplain, and vertically to groundwater.

docs.title: Peatland
docs.excerpt: A wetland where waterlogging slows decomposition enough that partially decayed plant material accumulates as peat.

docs.title: Canopy cover
docs.excerpt: The proportion of ground shaded by tree crowns, used with a land-use criterion to define forest statistically.

docs.title: Forest degradation
docs.excerpt: A reduction in a forest’s structure, biomass or function that stops short of conversion to another land use.

docs.title: Allometric equation
docs.excerpt: A statistical relationship used to estimate tree biomass from measurable dimensions such as diameter and height.

docs.title: Aboveground biomass
docs.excerpt: The mass of living plant material above the soil surface, usually expressed as dry weight or as carbon per hectare.

docs.title: Janzen–Connell hypothesis
docs.excerpt: The proposal that host-specific natural enemies near a parent tree suppress its own seedlings, making space for other species and maintaining diversity.

docs.title: Disturbance regime
docs.excerpt: The characteristic frequency, severity and spatial pattern of the disturbances a forest type experiences.

docs.title: Natural regeneration
docs.excerpt: Forest recovery from seed already present in or reaching a site, without planting.

docs.title: Boreal forest
docs.excerpt: The circumpolar coniferous forest belt of the northern high latitudes, also called taiga.

docs.title: Soil horizon
docs.excerpt: A layer within a soil profile distinguished by colour, texture, structure or composition from the layers above and below.

docs.title: State factors of soil formation (CLORPT)
docs.excerpt: The five factors — climate, organisms, relief, parent material and time — that together determine what soil forms at a site.

docs.title: Equivalent soil mass correction
docs.excerpt: A method of comparing soil carbon stocks by mass of soil rather than by fixed depth, to remove the effect of changing bulk density.

docs.title: Bulk density
docs.excerpt: The dry mass of soil per unit volume, including pore space.

docs.title: Microbial necromass
docs.excerpt: Dead microbial cell material, now understood to be a major component of stable soil organic carbon.

docs.title: Mycorrhiza
docs.excerpt: A symbiosis between a fungus and a plant root, in which the fungus supplies nutrients and water and receives carbon.

docs.title: Cation exchange capacity
docs.excerpt: The quantity of positively charged nutrients a soil can hold on the surfaces of clay and organic matter.

docs.title: Land degradation neutrality
docs.excerpt: A policy target under which losses in land condition are balanced by gains elsewhere within a given period.

docs.title: Soil erosion rate
docs.excerpt: The mass of soil removed from an area per unit time, usually reported in tonnes per hectare per year.

docs.title: Source–pathway–receptor
docs.excerpt: The framework that organises pollution analysis around where a substance comes from, how it travels, and what it reaches.

docs.title: Dose–response relationship
docs.excerpt: How the probability or severity of a health effect changes with the amount of exposure.

docs.title: PM2.5
docs.excerpt: Airborne particles with an aerodynamic diameter of 2.5 micrometres or less.

docs.title: Air quality index
docs.excerpt: A scale that converts measured pollutant concentrations into a single number and colour band.

docs.title: Nitrogen cascade
docs.excerpt: The sequence of effects a single atom of reactive nitrogen causes as it moves through air, water and soil before returning to inert N₂.

docs.title: Critical load
docs.excerpt: The deposition rate of a pollutant below which significant harmful effects on an ecosystem do not occur, according to present knowledge.

docs.title: Persistence, bioaccumulation and toxicity
docs.excerpt: The three screening properties used to decide whether a chemical warrants international control.

docs.title: Cold condensation
docs.excerpt: The tendency of semi-volatile pollutants to evaporate in warm regions and condense in cold ones, concentrating them at high latitudes.

docs.title: Methylmercury
docs.excerpt: The organic form of mercury produced by microorganisms in sediments and waters, and the form that biomagnifies.

docs.title: Artificial light at night
docs.excerpt: Anthropogenic illumination of the night environment, measured as sky brightness or as surface irradiance.

docs.title: Biodiversity
docs.excerpt: Variation in living systems at every level: genetic, species, functional and ecosystem.

docs.title: Ecosystem
docs.excerpt: A community of organisms together with the physical environment they exchange energy and matter with.

docs.title: Cell
docs.excerpt: The smallest unit carrying out the full set of processes life requires, bounded by a membrane.

docs.title: DNA
docs.excerpt: A double-stranded molecule storing heritable information as a sequence of four bases.

docs.title: Evolution
docs.excerpt: Change in the genetic composition of populations across generations.

docs.title: Natural selection
docs.excerpt: Differential reproduction of heritable variants, and the process by which populations become adapted.

docs.title: Thermodynamics
docs.excerpt: The science of energy, heat and work, and of what the laws governing them forbid.

docs.title: Entropy
docs.excerpt: A state function measuring the number of microscopic arrangements consistent with a system’s macroscopic state.

docs.title: Fluid mosaic model
docs.excerpt: The description of a biological membrane as a two-dimensional lipid fluid with proteins embedded and moving in it.

docs.title: Proton-motive force
docs.excerpt: The combined chemical and electrical gradient of protons across a membrane, used to drive ATP synthesis.

docs.title: Rubisco
docs.excerpt: The enzyme that fixes carbon dioxide in photosynthesis, and one of the slowest and least specific enzymes in wide use.

docs.title: Meiosis
docs.excerpt: The two-stage division that halves chromosome number and generates new combinations of alleles.

docs.title: Motor protein
docs.excerpt: A protein that converts chemical energy into directed movement along a cytoskeletal filament.

docs.title: C-value paradox
docs.excerpt: The absence of any consistent relationship between genome size and organismal complexity.

docs.title: Mismatch repair
docs.excerpt: A system that detects and corrects base-pairing errors left after DNA replication.

docs.title: De novo mutation
docs.excerpt: A genetic change present in an individual but not in either parent.

docs.title: DNA methylation
docs.excerpt: The addition of a methyl group to a cytosine base, altering gene expression without changing sequence.

docs.title: Missing heritability
docs.excerpt: The gap between heritability estimated from family studies and the fraction explained by identified genetic variants.

docs.title: Polygenic score
docs.excerpt: A single number summing many small genetic effects estimated from a genome-wide association study.

docs.title: Linkage disequilibrium
docs.excerpt: The non-random association of alleles at nearby loci, which lets a genotyped marker stand in for an unmeasured causal variant.

docs.title: Effective population size
docs.excerpt: The size of an idealised population that would lose genetic variation at the same rate as the population being studied.

docs.title: Nearly neutral theory
docs.excerpt: The proposal that a large class of mutations is weakly enough selected that both drift and selection govern their fate.

docs.title: Reproductive isolation
docs.excerpt: The barriers, before or after fertilisation, that prevent gene flow between populations.

docs.title: Homoplasy
docs.excerpt: Similarity between lineages that arose independently rather than from a common ancestor.

docs.title: Long-branch attraction
docs.excerpt: A systematic artefact in which rapidly evolving lineages are grouped together regardless of their true relationships.

docs.title: Incomplete lineage sorting
docs.excerpt: The persistence of ancestral genetic variation through successive speciation events, so that a gene tree disagrees with the species tree.

docs.title: Taxonomic inflation
docs.excerpt: An increase in recognised species counts caused by changing species concepts rather than by new discoveries.

docs.title: Binomial nomenclature
docs.excerpt: The convention of naming a species by a genus name followed by a specific epithet, governed by formal codes.

docs.title: Asgard archaea
docs.excerpt: A group of archaea whose genomes contain many features previously thought unique to eukaryotes.

docs.title: Alternation of generations
docs.excerpt: A life cycle alternating between a multicellular haploid phase and a multicellular diploid phase.

docs.title: Horizontal gene transfer
docs.excerpt: The movement of genetic material between organisms other than by descent from parent to offspring.

docs.title: Great plate count anomaly
docs.excerpt: The long-observed gap between the number of microbial cells visible under a microscope and the number that grow on culture media.

docs.title: 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing
docs.excerpt: A survey method that amplifies and sequences a conserved ribosomal gene to identify the bacteria and archaea present.

docs.title: Compositional data
docs.excerpt: Data expressing parts of a whole, in which the components sum to a constant and therefore cannot vary independently.

docs.title: Baltimore classification
docs.excerpt: A scheme grouping viruses by their genome type and the route they take to messenger RNA.

docs.title: Anammox
docs.excerpt: Anaerobic ammonium oxidation, a microbial process converting ammonium and nitrite directly to nitrogen gas.

docs.title: Countercurrent exchange
docs.excerpt: An arrangement in which two fluids flow in opposite directions, maintaining a gradient along the whole exchange surface.

docs.title: Oxygen dissociation curve
docs.excerpt: The sigmoid relationship between oxygen partial pressure and haemoglobin saturation.

docs.title: Starling forces
docs.excerpt: The balance of hydrostatic and osmotic pressures that determines fluid movement across a capillary wall.

docs.title: Thermal neutral zone
docs.excerpt: The range of ambient temperature over which an endotherm maintains body temperature without extra metabolic cost.

docs.title: Clonal selection
docs.excerpt: The principle that an antigen selects and expands the few lymphocytes whose receptors already bind it.

docs.title: Action potential
docs.excerpt: A rapid, self-propagating reversal of membrane voltage that carries a signal along a neuron.

docs.title: Morphogen gradient
docs.excerpt: A spatial concentration gradient of a signalling molecule that gives cells positional information during development.

docs.title: Water potential
docs.excerpt: The potential energy of water per unit volume, determining the direction in which water moves.

docs.title: Cohesion–tension mechanism
docs.excerpt: The explanation of sap ascent by evaporation at the leaf pulling a continuous water column held together by hydrogen bonding.

docs.title: Protospacer adjacent motif (PAM)
docs.excerpt: A short DNA sequence that must sit next to a target site for a CRISPR nuclease to cut it.

docs.title: Non-homologous end joining
docs.excerpt: A DNA repair pathway that rejoins broken ends directly, often with small insertions or deletions.

docs.title: Read length
docs.excerpt: The number of contiguous bases a sequencing platform determines in one pass.

docs.title: Predicted confidence score (pLDDT)
docs.excerpt: A per-residue confidence estimate produced alongside a predicted protein structure.

docs.title: Metabolic engineering
docs.excerpt: Redirecting a cell’s metabolism to produce a chosen compound, by adding, removing or tuning enzymatic steps.

docs.title: Substantial equivalence
docs.excerpt: A regulatory concept comparing an engineered crop with a conventional counterpart to decide what safety assessment is needed.

docs.title: Blackbody
docs.excerpt: An idealised object that absorbs all incident radiation and emits the maximum possible for its temperature.

docs.title: Optical depth
docs.excerpt: A dimensionless measure of how strongly a medium attenuates radiation passing through it.

docs.title: Effective emission height
docs.excerpt: The altitude from which outgoing infrared radiation effectively escapes to space.

docs.title: Band saturation
docs.excerpt: The condition in which a spectral absorption band already absorbs essentially all radiation at its centre.

docs.title: Lapse rate
docs.excerpt: The rate at which air temperature falls with height.

docs.title: Temperature inversion
docs.excerpt: A layer in which temperature rises with height, suppressing vertical mixing.

docs.title: Cloud condensation nuclei
docs.excerpt: Aerosol particles on which water vapour condenses to form cloud droplets.

docs.title: Convective available potential energy (CAPE)
docs.excerpt: The energy a rising air parcel would gain from buoyancy through the depth of the atmosphere.

docs.title: Coriolis effect
docs.excerpt: The apparent deflection of moving air or water in a rotating reference frame.

docs.title: Parameterisation
docs.excerpt: Representing a process too small or too complex to resolve on a model grid by a formula in terms of resolved variables.

docs.title: Seismic shadow zone
docs.excerpt: An angular band on the far side of the Earth where a given seismic wave type is not detected.

docs.title: Geodynamo
docs.excerpt: The convective motion of liquid iron in the outer core that generates Earth’s magnetic field.

docs.title: Betz limit
docs.excerpt: The theoretical maximum fraction of the kinetic energy in wind that a turbine can extract: 16/27, about 59 per cent.

docs.title: Capacity factor
docs.excerpt: Actual energy generated over a period divided by what would have been generated at full rated output.

docs.title: Levelised cost of electricity
docs.excerpt: The average cost per unit of electricity over a plant’s life, discounted to present value.

docs.title: Round-trip efficiency
docs.excerpt: The fraction of energy put into storage that is recovered on discharge.

docs.title: Grid inertia
docs.excerpt: The rotational kinetic energy stored in synchronous generators, which resists sudden changes in system frequency.

docs.title: Curtailment
docs.excerpt: Deliberately reducing available generation below what the resource would allow.

docs.title: Fill factor
docs.excerpt: The ratio of a solar cell’s maximum power to the product of its open-circuit voltage and short-circuit current.

docs.title: AM1.5 reference spectrum
docs.excerpt: The standard solar spectrum used to rate photovoltaic modules, representing sunlight through 1.5 atmospheres.

docs.title: Carnot efficiency
docs.excerpt: The maximum fraction of heat that any engine can convert to work between two temperatures.

docs.title: Exergy
docs.excerpt: The portion of an energy flow that can in principle be converted into useful work.

docs.title: State function
docs.excerpt: A property determined solely by a system’s current state, independent of the path taken to reach it.

docs.title: Emissivity
docs.excerpt: The ratio of a surface’s thermal emission to that of a blackbody at the same temperature.

docs.title: Reynolds number
docs.excerpt: The dimensionless ratio of inertial to viscous forces in a flow.

docs.title: Boundary layer
docs.excerpt: The thin region next to a surface where viscosity dominates and flow velocity changes from zero to the free-stream value.

docs.title: Group velocity
docs.excerpt: The speed at which the envelope of a wave packet — and therefore its energy and information — travels.

docs.title: Resonance
docs.excerpt: The large-amplitude response of a system driven at a frequency near its natural frequency.

docs.title: Rayleigh criterion
docs.excerpt: The condition for two point sources to be just resolvable, set by diffraction at the aperture.

docs.title: Decibel
docs.excerpt: A logarithmic unit expressing a ratio between two power or amplitude quantities.

docs.title: Measurement uncertainty
docs.excerpt: The quantified doubt attached to a measured value, without which a number is not a measurement.

docs.title: Metrological traceability
docs.excerpt: An unbroken chain of calibrations linking a measurement to a stated reference, usually the SI.

docs.title: Nuclear binding energy
docs.excerpt: The energy released when nucleons bind into a nucleus, expressed per nucleon.

docs.title: Becquerel, gray and sievert
docs.excerpt: Three radiation units measuring three different quantities: activity, absorbed dose and effective dose.

docs.title: Linear no-threshold model
docs.excerpt: The assumption that radiation risk is proportional to dose with no threshold below which risk is zero.

docs.title: Decay heat
docs.excerpt: Heat produced by radioactive decay of fission products after a reactor chain reaction has stopped.

docs.title: Fusion triple product
docs.excerpt: The product of plasma density, temperature and energy confinement time that a fusion device must exceed.

docs.title: Bandgap
docs.excerpt: The energy range between a solid’s filled and empty electronic states, in which no electron states exist.

docs.title: Doping
docs.excerpt: Deliberately adding impurity atoms to a semiconductor to control its conductivity.

docs.title: Five sigma
docs.excerpt: The statistical threshold conventionally required to claim a discovery in particle physics.

docs.title: Neutrino oscillation
docs.excerpt: The change of a neutrino between flavour states as it travels, which requires the neutrino to have mass.

docs.title: Wave–particle duality
docs.excerpt: The observation that quantum entities show wave-like or particle-like behaviour depending on what is measured.

docs.title: Decoherence
docs.excerpt: The loss of quantum coherence as a system becomes entangled with its environment.

docs.title: Quantum error correction
docs.excerpt: Encoding one logical qubit across many physical qubits so errors can be detected and corrected without measuring the state.

docs.title: Uncertainty relation
docs.excerpt: The bound on how precisely two conjugate quantities, such as position and momentum, can simultaneously be defined.
